text: Butter adds rich flavour and browns beautifully but burns at a lower temperature because of its milk solids, while oil tolerates higher heat but lacks butter's flavour. Cooks often combine them, or use clarified butter, to gain butter's taste with greater heat tolerance for searing and sautéing.

title: Toasted sesame oil
text: Toasted sesame oil is pressed from roasted sesame seeds and has an intense, nutty aroma. It is used as a finishing seasoning rather than a cooking oil, added at the end or to dressings and dips, because heat destroys its delicate fragrance. A small amount adds pronounced flavour to Asian dishes.

title: How vinegar is made
text: Vinegar is produced when bacteria ferment the alcohol in wine, cider or another base into acetic acid, giving the sour taste. Different bases yield different vinegars, from wine and cider to rice and malt. Its acidity brightens dishes, balances richness, and acts as a preservative in pickling and dressings.

title: Balsamic vinegar
text: Balsamic vinegar is made from cooked grape must, aged in wooden barrels to develop a dark colour and sweet-tart, syrupy character. Traditional balsamic from Modena is aged for years and intensely concentrated, while commercial versions are younger and thinner. It is used in dressings, reductions and drizzled over dishes and even fruit.

title: Rice vinegar
text: Rice vinegar is a mild, slightly sweet vinegar made from fermented rice, milder and less sharp than Western vinegars. It is essential to sushi rice, dressings and many East Asian dishes. Seasoned rice vinegar has added sugar and salt. Its gentle acidity brightens dishes without overpowering delicate flavours.

title: Making a vinaigrette
text: A vinaigrette is an emulsion of oil and an acid such as vinegar or citrus, typically around three parts oil to one part acid, seasoned with salt, pepper and often mustard, which helps it emulsify. Whisking or shaking disperses the oil into droplets. It can also be flavoured with shallot, herbs or honey.

title: Animal fats in cooking
text: Animal fats such as lard, duck fat, beef tallow and schmaltz carry deep, savoury flavour and have high smoke points that suit roasting and frying. Lard makes flaky pastry, duck fat crisps potatoes, and rendered chicken fat enriches many dishes. Each imparts a distinctive richness that vegetable oils cannot.

title: Storing oils
text: Oils degrade and turn rancid through exposure to heat, light and air, developing stale, unpleasant flavours. They are best stored in a cool, dark place in sealed containers, and delicate oils like nut and flaxseed oils benefit from refrigeration. Buying oils in quantities that will be used before they spoil avoids waste.

title: Beef cuts overview
text: Beef is divided into primal cuts whose location determines the best cooking method. Cuts from the little-worked back and loin, such as ribeye, sirloin, and tenderloin, are tender and suit fast dry-heat cooking. Hard-working cuts from the shoulder (chuck), leg (round), and shin are tougher, rich in connective tissue, and need long, moist, slow cooking to become tender.

title: Ribeye steak
text: The ribeye is cut from the rib primal and is prized for heavy marbling of intramuscular fat, which bastes the meat during cooking and gives rich flavour. It suits high-heat methods such as grilling, pan-searing, or roasting as a standing rib. Best cooked to medium-rare or medium so the fat renders; excessive doneness dries the lean portions.

title: Sirloin steak
text: Sirloin comes from the rear back between the loin and the rump. It balances tenderness and beefy flavour at a lower cost than fillet, and holds up well to grilling and pan-frying. Cook to medium-rare and rest before slicing across the grain to keep it tender.

title: Beef brisket
text: Brisket comes from the lower chest and is a tough, well-exercised cut laced with connective tissue and fat. It requires long, slow, moist cooking such as braising, pot-roasting, or barbecue smoking, over many hours, so the collagen breaks down into gelatin and the meat becomes tender. Slicing against the grain is essential.

title: Beef chuck
text: Chuck comes from the shoulder and is a flavourful but tough cut with abundant connective tissue. It is the classic choice for stews, braises, and pot roasts, and is often ground for burgers because its fat content gives juicy results. Long, gentle moist cooking dissolves the collagen and yields tender meat.

title: Beef short ribs
text: Short ribs are cut from the rib and plate sections and consist of meat layered over the rib bones with generous fat and connective tissue. They are ideally braised for several hours until the meat is fork-tender and falling from the bone. Korean-style short ribs (galbi) are cut thin across the bones and grilled quickly instead.

title: Beef shin and shank
text: Shin, or shank, is the leg muscle and is extremely tough but rich in collagen, which makes exceptionally gelatinous, silky braises and stocks. It is the traditional cut for osso buco when taken from veal. Cook very slowly in liquid until the meat is spoon-tender and the bone marrow softens.

title: Roasting a beef joint
text: A prime rib or sirloin joint is roasted by first browning the exterior at high heat, then lowering the oven to cook the interior evenly to the desired doneness measured with a thermometer. A joint on the bone cooks more evenly and stays juicier. Rest the joint at least fifteen minutes before carving across the grain.

title: Stir-frying beef
text: For stir-fried beef, slice a tender cut such as sirloin or flank thinly across the grain, then cook in small batches over very high heat so the pan stays hot and the meat sears rather than stews. Marinating with a little cornflour and soy, a technique called velveting, keeps the slices tender and moist.

title: Flank and skirt steak
text: Flank and skirt are thin, flavourful cuts from the belly and diaphragm with pronounced long grain. They are best cooked quickly over high heat to medium-rare, then sliced thinly against the grain to shorten the fibres and avoid toughness. Both take well to bold marinades and are classic for fajitas.

title: Ground beef safety
text: Grinding distributes surface bacteria throughout the meat, so ground beef must be cooked to an internal temperature of 71C (160F) to be safe, unlike whole steaks which can be served rare because bacteria remain on the exterior. Choose ground beef with around fifteen to twenty percent fat for juicy burgers.

title: Pork cuts overview
text: Pork primals include the shoulder, loin, belly, and leg. The loin is lean and tender for quick cooking, the shoulder and leg are tougher and suit slow roasting or braising, and the fatty belly is cured for bacon or slow-roasted for crackling. Modern pork is bred leaner, so loin cuts overcook easily.

title: Pork tenderloin
text: Pork tenderloin is a lean, tender muscle from the loin that cooks in minutes and dries out quickly if overdone. Sear it to brown the outside then finish in the oven to an internal temperature of about 63C (145F), followed by a short rest, which leaves the centre slightly pink and juicy.

title: Pork shoulder
text: Pork shoulder, sold as Boston butt or picnic, is a fatty, collagen-rich cut ideal for slow cooking. Roasted low and slow or braised for hours it becomes meltingly tender and is the classic cut for pulled pork, carnitas, and ragu. The fat keeps it moist through long cooking.

title: Pork belly and crackling
text: Pork belly is a layered cut of meat and fat that can be slow-roasted, braised, or cured. For crisp crackling, the skin must be scored, dried thoroughly, and salted, then started at high heat so the surface blisters and crisps before the oven is lowered to render the fat and cook the meat through.

title: Pork chops
text: Pork chops are cut from the loin and range from lean centre-cut to fattier rib and shoulder chops. Because modern loin is lean, chops are best cooked to just 63C (145F) with a short rest to stay juicy. Brining beforehand helps them retain moisture, and a good sear adds flavour.

title: Pork safe temperature
text: Guidance now allows whole cuts of pork to be cooked to an internal temperature of 63C (145F) followed by a three-minute rest, leaving the meat slightly pink and juicy. Ground pork and sausages should reach 71C (160F). Trichinosis risk in modern farmed pork is very low, so the old well-done rule is unnecessary.

title: Lamb cuts overview
text: Lamb primals include the shoulder, rack, loin, and leg. The rack and loin are tender for quick roasting or grilling, while the shoulder and shanks are tougher, collagen-rich cuts best braised or slow-roasted. Lamb has a distinctive flavour that pairs well with rosemary, garlic, mint, and warm spices.

title: Rack of lamb
text: A rack of lamb is a row of rib chops from the loin, often French-trimmed to expose the bones. It is tender and quick-cooking, best seared to brown the fat cap then roasted to medium-rare, about 55C (130F). Resting before carving into individual cutlets keeps it pink and juicy.

title: Leg of lamb
text: Leg of lamb can be roasted whole on the bone or boned and butterflied for even cooking and grilling. Studded with garlic and rosemary and roasted to medium-rare or medium, it stays succulent. Slow-roasting a leg for several hours instead yields meltingly tender meat that pulls apart.

title: Lamb shanks
text: Lamb shanks are the lower leg, a tough cut rich in connective tissue that rewards long, slow braising. Cooked gently in wine or stock with aromatics for a few hours, the collagen dissolves and the meat becomes tender enough to fall from the bone, yielding a rich, gelatinous sauce.

title: Lamb doneness
text: Lamb is commonly served pink: medium-rare is about 55C (130F) and medium about 60C (140F). Tender cuts such as rack, loin, and leg suit this range, while tough cuts such as shank and shoulder must instead be cooked well beyond that, slowly, until the connective tissue breaks down.

title: Slow cooking principles
text: Slow cooking uses low, gentle heat over a long period to transform tough, collagen-rich cuts into tender meat. The collagen in connective tissue converts to gelatin only above about 70C (160F) held for hours, which lubricates the meat. Moisture from braising liquid or the meat's own fat prevents drying during the long cook.

title: Browning meat for stews
text: Browning meat before braising develops flavour through the Maillard reaction, creating savoury, complex notes that plain simmering cannot. Pat the meat dry, brown it in batches so the pan stays hot, and deglaze the fond stuck to the pan with liquid to capture that flavour in the sauce.

title: Mince and ragu
text: Minced or ground meat forms the base of many dishes, from burgers to sauces. For a rich ragu, brown the mince well to build flavour, then simmer gently with aromatics and liquid so the fat and collagen enrich the sauce. Cooking mince slowly for a long time, as in bolognese, deepens its taste.

title: Chicken cuts overview
text: A whole chicken yields breast, thigh, drumstick, and wing, each suited to different cooking. Breast is lean and dries out if overcooked, while thighs and drumsticks are darker, fattier, and more forgiving, staying juicy through longer cooking. Wings are mostly skin and bone and crisp well when roasted or fried.

title: Spatchcocking poultry
text: Spatchcocking, or butterflying, means removing the backbone with shears and flattening the bird so it lies flat. This exposes more skin for crisping and lets the whole bird cook faster and more evenly, since the thick thighs and thin breast finish closer together. It suits grilling and high-heat roasting.

title: Chicken safe temperature
text: Poultry must reach an internal temperature of 74C (165F) at the thickest part to destroy salmonella and campylobacter, measured in the thigh for a whole bird. Because carryover cooking continues after removal, large birds can be pulled a few degrees early. Never rely on colour alone to judge doneness.

title: Chicken breast cookery
text: Skinless chicken breast is lean and overcooks easily, turning dry and stringy. Cook it gently to just 74C (165F), then rest. Pounding to an even thickness promotes uniform cooking, and poaching or pan-frying at moderate heat keeps it tender. A brief brine or marinade further guards against dryness.

title: Chicken thighs
text: Chicken thighs are dark meat with more fat and connective tissue than breast, which keeps them juicy and forgiving even when cooked past the minimum safe temperature. They suit braising, grilling, roasting, and curries. Bone-in, skin-on thighs deliver the most flavour and crisp skin.

title: Duck breast cookery
text: Duck breast has a thick fat layer under the skin. Score the skin in a crosshatch without cutting the meat, then start it skin-side down in a cold, dry pan over gentle heat so the fat renders slowly and the skin crisps. Cook the meat to medium-rare, as duck breast is best served pink.

title: Roasting duck
text: A whole duck is fatty, so the skin is pricked and the bird roasted at moderate heat for a long time to render the fat and crisp the skin, with the rendered fat poured off periodically. The legs need longer cooking than the breast, so the confit or two-stage approach is common for even results.

title: Roasting turkey
text: Turkey is a large, lean bird whose breast cooks faster than the thighs, so it easily dries out. Brining, shielding the breast with foil, or cooking the legs separately helps. Roast until the thigh reaches 74C (165F), then rest at least thirty minutes, since a large bird retains heat and carries over significantly.

title: Confit technique
text: Confit slowly cooks meat, classically duck or goose legs, fully submerged in fat at a low temperature until tender, then stores it sealed under that fat. The gentle cooking makes the meat succulent, and the fat seal preserves it for weeks. Confit legs are usually crisped in a hot pan before serving.

title: Filleting a round fish
text: To fillet a round fish, cut behind the gills down to the backbone, then run the knife along the spine from head to tail, keeping the blade flat against the bones to lift off the fillet in one piece. Repeat on the other side, then remove the pin bones with tweezers and trim the belly.

title: Pan-frying fish fillets
text: For crisp-skinned fish, dry the fillet, season it, and place it skin-side down in a hot oiled pan, pressing briefly so it stays flat. Cook mostly on the skin side until the flesh turns opaque up the sides, then flip for a moment to finish. Overcooking makes fish dry and tough.

title: Grilling fish
text: Firm, oily fish such as tuna, salmon, mackerel, and swordfish grill best because they hold together over high heat. Oil the fish and the grate, and avoid moving the fish until it releases cleanly, which signals a set crust. Whole fish grill well and the skin protects the flesh.

title: Fish en papillote
text: En papillote cooks fish sealed in a parcel of parchment or foil with aromatics, vegetables, and a splash of liquid or wine. The trapped steam cooks the fish gently and infuses it with flavour while keeping it moist. The parcel is opened at the table to release the fragrant steam.

title: Cooking prawns
text: Prawns and shrimp cook very fast and turn tough and rubbery if overdone. They are ready when the flesh turns opaque and curls into a loose C shape; a tight O shape means overcooked. Cook them over high heat by sauteing, grilling, or poaching for just a couple of minutes.

title: Cooking squid
text: Squid becomes tender either with very quick, high-heat cooking of a minute or two, as in frying or grilling, or with long, slow braising of forty minutes or more. The middle ground turns it rubbery. Scoring the flesh helps it cook evenly and curl attractively.

title: Smoked fish
text: Cold-smoked fish such as smoked salmon is cured and smoked below about 30C, so it stays raw in texture and is eaten as is. Hot-smoked fish such as smoked mackerel or hot-smoked salmon is cooked through by the smoking heat and flakes readily. Both add rich, savoury depth to dishes.

title: Fish doneness
text: Most fish is done when the flesh turns from translucent to opaque and just begins to flake when gently pressed, roughly 50 to 60C internally. Tuna is often served rare in the centre. Because fish overcooks quickly, it is better pulled from the heat slightly early and allowed to finish by carryover.

title: Cooking scallops
text: Scallops are seared quickly over high heat to caramelise the surface while keeping the centre just cooked and translucent. Dry them thoroughly first, since surface moisture steams rather than sears. A minute or so per side is enough; overcooked scallops turn rubbery and lose their sweetness.

title: Pasta carbonara
text: Carbonara is a Roman pasta dish of spaghetti or rigatoni dressed with a sauce of egg yolks, grated Pecorino Romano, and rendered guanciale, seasoned with black pepper. The heat of the drained pasta and a little starchy cooking water cook the eggs into a creamy sauce off the heat. It contains no cream.

title: Cacio e pepe
text: Cacio e pepe is a Roman pasta of just three elements: pasta, Pecorino Romano, and black pepper. Grated cheese is emulsified with hot, starchy pasta water off direct heat to form a smooth, creamy sauce that coats the pasta, while toasted pepper adds aroma and bite. Careful temperature control prevents the cheese clumping.

title: Pasta amatriciana
text: Amatriciana is a Roman-Lazio sauce of guanciale, tomato, and Pecorino Romano, finished with black pepper and sometimes a little chilli. The guanciale is rendered until crisp, tomatoes are added and simmered, and the sauce is tossed with bucatini or spaghetti. It shares roots with the pre-tomato gricia.

title: Ragu alla bolognese
text: Ragu alla bolognese is a slow-cooked meat sauce from Bologna made with minced beef and often pork, a soffritto of onion, carrot, and celery, a little tomato, and milk or wine, simmered gently for hours. It is traditionally served with fresh tagliatelle or in lasagne, not with spaghetti.

title: Pesto alla genovese
text: Pesto alla genovese is an uncooked Ligurian sauce of fresh basil, pine nuts, garlic, Parmesan and Pecorino, and olive oil, traditionally ground in a mortar and pestle. It classically dresses trofie or trenette pasta, often with potatoes and green beans. Gentle handling keeps the basil from oxidising and darkening.

title: Aglio e olio
text: Spaghetti aglio e olio is a simple Neapolitan dish of spaghetti tossed with garlic gently fried in olive oil, often with chilli flakes and parsley. The garlic is cooked slowly until golden but not burnt, and a little pasta water is added to emulsify the oil into a light sauce that clings to the pasta.

title: Lasagne alla bolognese
text: Lasagne alla bolognese layers sheets of pasta with ragu, bechamel, and Parmesan, then bakes until bubbling and golden. The bechamel and ragu together keep the dish moist and rich. In the classic Emilian version spinach pasta is used, and the assembled dish rests briefly before cutting so the layers hold.

title: Pasta puttanesca
text: Puttanesca is a bold Neapolitan sauce of tomatoes, garlic, anchovies, capers, olives, and chilli, tossed with spaghetti. The anchovies melt into the oil to add savoury depth without tasting fishy, and the capers and olives bring salt and tang. It cooks quickly and needs little added salt.

title: Pasta arrabbiata
text: Penne all'arrabbiata is a spicy Roman tomato sauce whose name means angry, referring to the heat of dried chilli. Garlic and chilli are gently cooked in olive oil, tomatoes are added and simmered until thick, and the sauce is finished with parsley and tossed with penne. It is deliberately simple and fiery.

title: Pasta primavera
text: Pasta primavera is a dish of pasta tossed with an assortment of fresh spring vegetables, lightly cooked to stay crisp and colourful. It is usually dressed with olive oil or a light cream or butter sauce and Parmesan. The vegetables are added according to cooking time so all finish tender-crisp together.

title: Bechamel sauce
text: Bechamel is one of the five French mother sauces, made by cooking a white roux of butter and flour, then whisking in milk until it thickens into a smooth white sauce. It is seasoned with salt, white pepper, and nutmeg, and forms the base of dishes such as lasagne, gratins, and croque monsieur.

title: Veloute sauce
text: Veloute is a mother sauce made by thickening a light stock, such as chicken, veal, or fish, with a blond roux. The result is a smooth, pale sauce that serves as a base for many derivatives, including sauce supreme with cream and allemande enriched with egg yolk. The stock's quality defines its flavour.

title: Tomato mother sauce
text: The classic tomato mother sauce is built from tomatoes cooked with aromatics and, in the older French style, a roux and stock, though modern versions rely on the tomatoes themselves for body. It is a base for countless dishes and derivatives. Long, gentle simmering deepens and sweetens the flavour.

title: Pan sauce technique
text: A pan sauce is made in the pan used to cook meat by deglazing the browned fond with wine, stock, or another liquid, scraping up the flavourful residue, then reducing and often finishing with butter for gloss and body. It captures the meat's flavour and turns it into a quick, complementary sauce.

title: Gravy from drippings
text: Gravy is made from the fat and juices left after roasting meat. The drippings are combined with flour to form a roux, then whisked with stock and the deglazed pan juices and simmered until thickened and smooth. Straining and careful seasoning give a glossy, savoury sauce for the roast.

title: Vinaigrette
text: A vinaigrette is an emulsion of oil and an acid such as vinegar or lemon juice, seasoned with salt, pepper, and often mustard, which helps stabilise the mixture. A classic ratio is about three parts oil to one part acid. Whisking or shaking disperses the oil into droplets to form a temporary emulsion.

title: Mayonnaise
text: Mayonnaise is a stable cold emulsion of oil suspended in egg yolk, with lemon juice or vinegar and seasoning. Oil is added very slowly at first while whisking so the yolk's lecithin can coat each droplet. Adding oil too fast, or too cold ingredients, causes the emulsion to break.

title: Salsa verde
text: Salsa verde is a green herb sauce; the Italian version blends parsley, capers, anchovies, garlic, vinegar, and olive oil into a piquant condiment for meat and fish. The Mexican salsa verde is different, made from tomatillos, chilli, onion, and coriander. Both are uncooked or lightly cooked and bright in flavour.

title: Chimichurri
text: Chimichurri is an Argentine uncooked sauce of finely chopped parsley, garlic, oregano, red wine vinegar, chilli flakes, and olive oil. Bright, herbaceous, and tangy, it is the classic accompaniment to grilled beef. Letting it sit briefly before serving allows the flavours to meld.

title: Gluten in bread
text: Gluten is a network of proteins formed when wheat flour is mixed with water and worked. It gives bread dough elasticity and strength, trapping the carbon dioxide produced by yeast so the loaf rises and holds its structure. Kneading develops gluten, while resting relaxes it; bread flour has more gluten-forming protein than plain flour.

title: Yeast fermentation in dough
text: Yeast ferments the sugars in dough, producing carbon dioxide gas and alcohol. The gas is trapped by the gluten network, causing the dough to rise, while fermentation also develops flavour. Warmth speeds fermentation and cold slows it; a long, slow rise builds more complex taste in the finished bread.

title: Proving dough
text: Proving, or proofing, is the rest during which shaped or mixed dough rises as the yeast produces gas. Under-proved dough is dense and bursts unevenly; over-proved dough collapses because the gluten can no longer hold the gas. A properly proved dough springs back slowly when gently pressed.

title: No-knead bread
text: No-knead bread relies on a very long, slow fermentation of a wet dough instead of kneading to develop gluten and flavour. The dough rests many hours so the gluten forms on its own, then is baked in a preheated covered pot, which traps steam to give a crisp crust and open crumb.

title: Focaccia
text: Focaccia is a flat Italian yeast bread made from a wet, olive-oil-rich dough. After proving, it is dimpled with the fingers, drizzled with oil, and often topped with salt, rosemary, or vegetables, then baked until golden. The high hydration and generous oil give a soft, open interior and crisp base.

title: Ciabatta
text: Ciabatta is an Italian bread made from a very wet, slack dough, often started with a pre-ferment called a biga, which gives its open, holey crumb and chewy texture. The dough is handled gently to preserve the gas bubbles, and the loaves are shaped into flat slippers, from which the name comes.

title: Sourdough basics
text: Sourdough is leavened by a starter of flour and water hosting wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria instead of commercial yeast. The bacteria produce acids that give the characteristic tang and help preserve the loaf, while the wild yeast provides the rise. Fermentation is slower and needs a mature, active starter.

title: Flatbreads
text: Flatbreads are thin breads that may be leavened or unleavened, such as pita, naan, chapati, and tortilla. Many are cooked quickly at high heat on a griddle, in a tandoor, or in a very hot oven. Pita puffs into a pocket as trapped steam inflates the thin dough.

title: Pizza dough
text: Pizza dough is a simple yeast dough of flour, water, salt, and yeast, developed to form gluten and fermented, often slowly and cold, for flavour and extensibility. It is stretched by hand rather than rolled to preserve the airy edge, then baked at very high heat so the base crisps and the rim chars and puffs.

title: Caramelisation
text: Caramelisation is the browning of sugar when heated above about 160C, breaking it down into nutty, bitter, and sweet aromatic compounds and a brown colour. Unlike the Maillard reaction it involves only sugar and no protein. It develops flavour in caramel, roasted vegetables, and the crust of baked goods.

title: Puff pastry
text: Puff pastry is a laminated dough in which a block of butter is folded into dough repeatedly to create hundreds of thin alternating layers. In the oven the water in the butter turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, making the pastry rise into crisp, flaky sheets. It must stay cold to keep the layers distinct.

title: Sponge cake method
text: A whisked sponge relies on air beaten into eggs, or eggs and sugar, for its rise rather than chemical leaveners. The foam is folded gently with flour to avoid knocking out air, then baked while the trapped air expands and sets. Overmixing deflates the batter and yields a dense cake.

title: Making meringue
text: Meringue is made by whisking egg whites with sugar until stiff and glossy. The whipping unfolds the proteins to trap air, and sugar stabilises the foam. Clean, grease-free bowls are essential, as any fat prevents the whites foaming. French, Italian, and Swiss meringues differ in how the sugar is added.

title: Pastry cream
text: Pastry cream, or creme patissiere, is a thick custard stabilised with flour or cornflour so it can be piped and holds its shape. Egg yolks, sugar, and starch are whisked, hot milk is added, and the mixture is cooked until it thickens and the starch removes the risk of curdling. It fills tarts, eclairs, and cakes.

title: Making caramel
text: Caramel is made by heating sugar, with or without water, until it melts and browns into an amber liquid. The darker it cooks the more bitter and complex it becomes, but it burns quickly once dark. Adding cream or butter off the heat makes caramel sauce; the hot sugar can cause serious burns.

title: Chocolate tempering
text: Tempering chocolate controls the crystallisation of cocoa butter so the set chocolate is glossy, snaps cleanly, and does not develop dull bloom. It involves melting, cooling to encourage stable crystals, then gently rewarming to a precise working temperature. Untempered chocolate sets soft and streaky.

title: Tiramisu
text: Tiramisu is an Italian dessert of coffee-soaked ladyfinger biscuits layered with a cream of mascarpone, egg, and sugar, dusted with cocoa. The biscuits are dipped briefly so they soften without disintegrating, and the assembled dish is chilled so the layers set and the flavours meld. It is not baked.

title: Panna cotta
text: Panna cotta is an Italian set cream dessert made by warming cream with sugar and flavourings, dissolving gelatin into it, then chilling until just set. It should be barely firm enough to hold its shape yet wobble and melt on the tongue. Too much gelatin makes it rubbery.

title: Creme brulee
text: Creme brulee is a baked custard of cream, egg yolks, sugar, and vanilla, cooked gently in a water bath until just set, then chilled. Before serving, a thin layer of sugar on top is caramelised with a torch or grill to form a brittle glass-like crust that cracks under a spoon.

title: Blind baking pastry
text: Blind baking is pre-baking a pastry case before adding a wet filling, so the base cooks through and stays crisp. The lined case is weighted with baking beans or rice to stop it puffing and slumping, baked until set, then the weights are removed to finish browning the base.

title: Boiling eggs
text: Boiling time sets the texture of an egg: a soft-boiled egg with a runny yolk takes about six minutes in simmering water, while a firm hard-boiled egg takes around ten to twelve. Cooling boiled eggs quickly in cold water stops cooking and prevents a grey-green ring forming around the yolk.

title: Poaching eggs
text: A poached egg is cooked out of its shell in barely simmering water, ideally a very fresh egg so the white holds together. A splash of vinegar helps the white set, and swirling the water gathers it around the yolk. The egg is done when the white is set but the yolk still runny, about three minutes.

title: Frittata
text: A frittata is an Italian open omelette in which beaten eggs are combined with fillings such as vegetables, cheese, or meat and cooked slowly, started on the stove and finished under a grill or in the oven. Unlike a folded omelette it is thick, set throughout, and cut into wedges.

title: Whisking egg whites
text: Egg whites whip into a foam when their proteins unfold and trap air. They reach soft peaks that flop over, then stiff peaks that stand upright. Any trace of fat or yolk prevents proper foaming, and over-whisking makes the foam dry and grainy. A pinch of acid such as cream of tartar stabilises the foam.

title: Chicken stock
text: Chicken stock is made by gently simmering chicken bones, often with a mirepoix of onion, carrot, and celery and aromatics, for a few hours. Skimming impurities and never boiling hard keeps it clear. Roasting the bones first gives a deeper brown stock, while raw bones make a lighter white stock.

title: Beef stock
text: Beef stock is made by simmering beef bones, usually roasted for colour and flavour, with vegetables and aromatics for many hours to extract gelatin and taste. A long, gentle simmer draws body from the collagen-rich bones, and regular skimming keeps it clear. It forms the base of brown sauces and hearty soups.

title: Vegetable stock
text: Vegetable stock is a quick, light stock made by simmering aromatic vegetables such as onion, carrot, celery, and leek with herbs for under an hour, since longer cooking dulls the flavour. Avoiding starchy or strongly coloured vegetables keeps it clear and clean-tasting. It suits vegetarian dishes and light soups.

title: Fish stock
text: Fish stock, or fumet, is made from the bones and heads of white fish simmered briefly, usually only twenty to thirty minutes, since longer cooking turns it bitter. Aromatics and sometimes white wine are added. Only lean white fish bones are used, as oily fish make the stock strong and greasy.

title: Minestrone
text: Minestrone is a hearty Italian vegetable soup that varies by season and region, typically combining beans, seasonal vegetables, and often pasta or rice in a tomato and vegetable broth. It begins with a soffritto and simmers until the vegetables are tender. Parmesan rind added while cooking deepens its savoury flavour.

title: French onion soup
text: French onion soup is made by cooking sliced onions slowly until deeply caramelised, then simmering them in beef stock, often with a splash of wine. It is served topped with toasted bread and melted Gruyere, browned under the grill. The long caramelisation of the onions gives the soup its sweet, rich depth.

title: Chowder
text: Chowder is a thick, chunky soup, classically of seafood such as clams or fish, or of corn, enriched with potatoes and often cream or milk. New England clam chowder is creamy and white, while Manhattan style is tomato-based. It is thickened by the potatoes and sometimes a little roux.

title: Gazpacho
text: Gazpacho is a cold Spanish soup from Andalusia, blended raw from ripe tomatoes, cucumber, pepper, garlic, bread, olive oil, and vinegar. Served chilled, it is refreshing in hot weather. The bread and oil give body and a silky texture when blended, and it is seasoned generously and rested to develop flavour.

title: Consomme
text: Consomme is a crystal-clear, intensely flavoured soup made by clarifying a rich stock. A raft of egg whites and minced meat is simmered in the stock, trapping the particles that cloud it as it rises, then the liquid is strained. The result is a refined, transparent broth.

title: Pureeing soups
text: Pureed soups are blended smooth after the ingredients are cooked tender, giving a velvety texture without added thickeners. Starchy vegetables such as potato or the ingredient itself provide body. Blending hot liquid requires care to vent steam and avoid splashing, and passing through a sieve makes the texture especially fine.

title: Coriander herb
text: Coriander leaf, known as cilantro in North America, is a bright, citrusy herb central to Mexican, Indian, and Southeast Asian cooking. Its flavour fades with heat, so it is usually added at the end or raw. The seeds are a warm, citrusy spice used quite differently from the fresh leaves.

title: Oregano
text: Oregano is a pungent Mediterranean herb, more robust than its relative marjoram, with a peppery, slightly bitter warmth. It is central to Italian, Greek, and Mexican cooking, flavouring tomato sauces, pizza, and grilled meats. Unusually among herbs, dried oregano is more intense and widely used than fresh.

title: Mint
text: Mint is a cooling, sweet herb used in both savoury and sweet dishes across Middle Eastern, North African, and British cooking. It flavours sauces for lamb, salads such as tabbouleh, yoghurt dishes, teas, and desserts. It is delicate and usually added fresh rather than cooked for long.

title: Sage
text: Sage is a soft, grey-green herb with a strong, earthy, slightly peppery flavour that suits rich, fatty foods. It pairs classically with pork, poultry stuffing, and butter sauces for pasta such as ravioli. Its robust flavour holds up to cooking, and fried sage leaves make a crisp garnish.

title: Dill
text: Dill is a feathery herb with a fresh, grassy, slightly aniseed flavour used widely in Scandinavian, Eastern European, and Middle Eastern cooking. It pairs classically with fish, especially salmon, with cucumber, potatoes, and yoghurt, and flavours pickles. Its delicate fronds are added near the end of cooking.

title: Coriander seed
text: Coriander seed is a warm, citrusy, mildly sweet spice, quite distinct from the fresh leaf of the same plant. It is a foundational spice in Indian and Middle Eastern blends and is often toasted and ground before use. It pairs well with cumin and features in curry powders and pickling spice.

title: Ginger spice
text: Ginger is a pungent, warm, slightly sweet rhizome used fresh, dried, and ground. Fresh ginger is sharp and juicy, central to Asian cooking, while dried ground ginger is warmer and used in baking. It pairs with garlic and chilli in savoury dishes and with cinnamon and clove in sweet ones.

title: Chilli heat
text: The heat of chilli peppers comes from capsaicin, concentrated in the white pith and seeds. Heat is measured on the Scoville scale, from mild bell peppers to fiery habaneros and beyond. Capsaicin is fat- and alcohol-soluble but not water-soluble, so dairy relieves chilli burn better than water.

title: Curry powder
text: Curry powder is a British-devised blend approximating Indian spice mixtures, usually built around turmeric, coriander, cumin, fenugreek, and chilli. Turmeric gives it the characteristic yellow colour. It is a convenience blend rather than a single authentic Indian spice, and toasting or blooming it improves its flavour.

title: Chinese five-spice
text: Chinese five-spice is a balanced blend, classically of star anise, fennel, clove, cinnamon, and Sichuan pepper, giving a warm, sweet, and slightly liquorice-like aroma. It is used in Chinese roasted and braised meats such as duck and pork. Its intensity means it is used sparingly.

title: Herbes de Provence
text: Herbes de Provence is a southern French blend of dried herbs, typically thyme, rosemary, oregano, savory, and marjoram, sometimes with lavender. It flavours grilled meats, roasted vegetables, and stews, evoking the herbs that grow wild in the region. It is usually added during cooking to release its aroma.

title: Toasting and blooming spices
text: Toasting whole spices in a dry pan or blooming ground spices in hot oil releases their volatile aromatic oils and deepens their flavour before they join a dish. Toasting is done briefly over moderate heat until fragrant, taking care not to scorch them, which turns the spices bitter.

title: Risotto method
text: Risotto is made by toasting short-grain rice such as Arborio in fat, then adding hot stock a ladle at a time while stirring, so the starch releases gradually into a creamy sauce while the grains stay al dente. It is finished off the heat with butter and Parmesan, a step called mantecatura, for richness and gloss.

title: Paella
text: Paella is a Spanish rice dish from Valencia cooked in a wide, shallow pan so the rice forms a thin layer. Short-grain rice absorbs a saffron-scented stock along with ingredients such as rabbit, chicken, beans, or seafood. The rice is not stirred, allowing a prized caramelised crust called socarrat to form on the base.

title: Coq au vin
text: Coq au vin is a French braise of chicken cooked slowly in red wine with mushrooms, onions, and lardons of bacon. Traditionally an older, tougher bird was used, benefiting from long cooking, and the sauce is thickened by reduction and sometimes a little flour. The wine gives a deep, rich sauce.

title: Beef bourguignon
text: Beef bourguignon is a French braise of beef cooked slowly in red wine with mushrooms, pearl onions, and bacon lardons. Tough beef such as chuck is browned, then simmered gently for hours until tender in a wine-based sauce enriched by the meat's collagen. It is a classic of Burgundian cooking.

title: Ratatouille
text: Ratatouille is a Provencal stew of summer vegetables, typically aubergine, courgette, pepper, onion, and tomato, cooked with garlic and herbs in olive oil. Cooking the vegetables separately before combining, or layering them, keeps their flavours distinct. It can be served hot or at room temperature.

title: Bouillabaisse
text: Bouillabaisse is a Provencal fish stew from Marseille, made with several kinds of fish and shellfish simmered in a broth flavoured with saffron, fennel, tomato, and orange peel. It is traditionally served with rouille, a garlicky saffron mayonnaise, spread on toasted bread. The variety of fish is central to its character.

title: Cassoulet
text: Cassoulet is a rich, slow-cooked French casserole from the Languedoc of white beans baked with meats such as sausage, pork, and confit duck or goose. It cooks slowly for hours, developing a crust on top that is traditionally broken and stirred back in several times. It is hearty and deeply savoury.

title: Paella socarrat
text: Socarrat is the prized layer of toasted, caramelised rice that forms on the base of a paella when the liquid has been absorbed and the pan is left over heat a little longer. Listening for a gentle crackle and smelling toasting rice signals it is forming; it should be golden and crisp, not burnt.

title: Spanish tortilla
text: The Spanish tortilla, or tortilla espanola, is a thick omelette of eggs, potatoes, and often onion. The potatoes are cooked gently in oil until soft, mixed with beaten egg, and cooked slowly in a pan, then flipped to set both sides. It is served in wedges, warm or at room temperature.

title: Gazpacho and salmorejo
text: Salmorejo is a thicker, creamier Andalusian cold soup than gazpacho, made from tomatoes, bread, garlic, and olive oil blended smooth, without the cucumber and pepper of gazpacho. It is typically garnished with chopped hard-boiled egg and jamon. Its richness comes from a higher proportion of bread and oil.

title: Greek moussaka
text: Moussaka is a Greek baked dish of layered aubergine, a spiced lamb or beef tomato sauce, and a thick bechamel or custard topping, baked until golden. The aubergine is usually fried or roasted first. The rich meat layer is often spiced with cinnamon and allspice, distinguishing it from an Italian bake.

title: Greek tzatziki
text: Tzatziki is a Greek dip and sauce of thick strained yoghurt, grated cucumber, garlic, olive oil, and often dill or mint. The cucumber is salted and squeezed to remove water so the sauce stays thick. It accompanies grilled meats, is served as a meze, and cools spicy or rich dishes.

title: Greek souvlaki
text: Souvlaki is Greek grilled meat, usually pork or chicken, marinated in olive oil, lemon, garlic, and oregano, then skewered and grilled over high heat. It is often served in or with pita alongside tzatziki, salad, and onions. The lemon and oregano marinade is characteristic of Greek grilling.

title: Hummus
text: Hummus is a Middle Eastern dip of cooked chickpeas blended with tahini, lemon juice, garlic, and olive oil until smooth. Cooking the chickpeas until very soft, and sometimes removing their skins, gives an especially creamy texture. It is typically finished with olive oil, paprika, and a sprinkle of whole chickpeas.

title: Falafel
text: Falafel are deep-fried patties or balls of ground chickpeas or fava beans mixed with herbs, garlic, and spices such as cumin and coriander. Crucially the pulses are soaked but not cooked before grinding, which gives falafel their firm, crisp texture. Cooked chickpeas would make the mixture fall apart in the oil.

title: Tabbouleh
text: Tabbouleh is a Levantine salad dominated by finely chopped parsley, with mint, tomato, spring onion, and a small amount of soaked bulgur wheat, dressed with lemon juice and olive oil. Contrary to some Western versions, it is a herb salad with a little grain, not a grain salad with herbs.

title: Shakshuka
text: Shakshuka is a dish of eggs poached in a spiced tomato and pepper sauce, popular across North Africa and the Middle East. The sauce is simmered with onion, garlic, cumin, and paprika, then wells are made and eggs cracked in to poach in the sauce. It is served bubbling from the pan with bread.

title: Chicken tikka masala
text: Chicken tikka masala consists of pieces of marinated, grilled chicken tikka in a creamy, mildly spiced tomato sauce. The chicken is marinated in yoghurt and spices and cooked in a hot oven or tandoor, then simmered in a sauce of tomato, cream, and warm spices. It is a popular British-Indian dish.

title: Rogan josh
text: Rogan josh is a Kashmiri curry of lamb or goat braised slowly in a sauce coloured red, traditionally by Kashmiri chillies and the flower dye ratanjot rather than by great heat. It is aromatic with spices such as cardamom, clove, cinnamon, and fennel, and yoghurt is often used to enrich the sauce.

title: Dal
text: Dal refers both to dried pulses such as lentils and to the dishes made from them across the Indian subcontinent. The pulses are simmered until soft, then flavoured with a tempering of spices bloomed in hot fat, called tarka or tadka, stirred through at the end. It is a staple protein source and comfort food.

title: Biryani
text: Biryani is a layered rice dish of the Indian subcontinent in which spiced, marinated meat or vegetables and partly cooked basmati rice are layered and cooked together, often sealed and finished by slow steaming called dum. The technique keeps the rice grains separate and infuses them with the spiced juices below.

title: Tempering spices for dal
text: Tarka, or tempering, is the Indian technique of frying whole and ground spices, and often garlic, chilli, or curry leaves, in hot oil or ghee until fragrant, then pouring the sizzling mixture over a finished dish such as dal. The hot fat extracts and carries the spices' aromas into the dish.

title: Naan bread
text: Naan is a soft, leavened Indian flatbread traditionally slapped onto the wall of a hot tandoor oven, where it puffs and blisters quickly. The dough is often enriched with yoghurt, milk, or egg for softness. At home it is cooked on a very hot griddle or under a grill to mimic the tandoor's heat.

title: Stir-frying technique
text: Stir-frying cooks small, uniform pieces of food quickly over very high heat in a wok while tossing constantly. Ingredients are prepared and organised in advance because cooking is fast, and they are added in order of cooking time. The intense heat that gives the characteristic aroma called wok hei needs a hot wok and dry ingredients.

title: Kung pao chicken
text: Kung pao chicken is a Sichuan stir-fry of diced chicken with peanuts, dried chillies, and Sichuan peppercorns in a savoury, slightly sweet and sour sauce. The Sichuan peppercorns give a tingling, numbing sensation that pairs with the chilli heat, a combination known as mala. It is cooked fast over high heat.

title: Mapo tofu
text: Mapo tofu is a Sichuan dish of soft tofu in a spicy, savoury sauce of fermented broad bean paste, chilli, and Sichuan pepper, usually with minced meat. It balances the numbing mala heat with the silky tofu, and is thickened lightly with starch. It is served with rice and bright in colour.

title: Fried rice technique
text: Fried rice is best made with cold, cooked rice, ideally a day old, because fresh warm rice is too moist and clumps. The dry grains fry and separate in a hot wok with a little oil, and ingredients are added quickly. Cooking over high heat keeps the rice from turning soggy.

title: Sichuan mala flavour
text: Mala is the signature flavour of Sichuan cuisine, combining the numbing, tingling sensation of Sichuan peppercorns with the heat of chilli. The peppercorns contain a compound that causes a distinctive buzzing on the lips and tongue, while chilli brings burning heat. The two together define dishes such as mapo tofu.

title: Sushi rice
text: Sushi rice is short-grain rice seasoned after cooking with a mixture of rice vinegar, sugar, and salt, then cooled to body temperature while being gently folded. The seasoning gives it a subtle tang and gloss, and the sticky grains hold together. The quality of the rice is central to good sushi.

title: Dashi stock
text: Dashi is the foundational Japanese stock, most commonly made by steeping kombu seaweed and then bonito flakes in hot water for a short time. It provides a deep savoury umami flavour with a light body and underpins miso soup, simmered dishes, and many sauces. It is quick to make and not boiled hard.

title: Miso soup
text: Miso soup is made by dissolving fermented soybean paste, miso, into warm dashi, usually with additions such as tofu and wakah seaweed and spring onion. The miso is stirred in off the boil, because boiling miso dulls its flavour and aroma and can make it grainy. It is a staple of Japanese meals.

title: Tempura
text: Tempura is a Japanese method of deep-frying seafood and vegetables in a light, cold batter of flour and ice-cold water, mixed minimally so it stays lumpy and gluten does not develop. The cold, barely mixed batter fries into a crisp, lacy, delicate coating. The oil must be hot so the coating stays light.

title: Teriyaki
text: Teriyaki is a Japanese cooking method in which food, often fish or chicken, is glazed with a sauce of soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar and grilled or pan-cooked until the sauce reduces to a shiny glaze. The name refers to the lustrous shine the reducing sauce gives the finished dish.

title: Ramen broth
text: Ramen is a Japanese noodle soup defined largely by its broth, which ranges from clear shio and shoyu styles to the rich, cloudy tonkotsu made by boiling pork bones hard for many hours to emulsify their collagen and fat. A seasoning base called tare and toppings complete the bowl.

title: Pad thai
text: Pad thai is a Thai stir-fried rice noodle dish combining a sweet, sour, and salty sauce of tamarind, fish sauce, and palm sugar with noodles, egg, tofu or shrimp, bean sprouts, and peanuts. The soaked noodles are stir-fried fast so they stay separate, and lime and peanuts finish the dish.

title: Thai green curry
text: Thai green curry is made from a paste of green chillies, lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime, garlic, and shrimp paste, fried in coconut cream then simmered with coconut milk, meat or vegetables, and fish sauce. Frying the paste first, called cracking, releases its aroma. Thai basil and lime finish it.

title: Balancing Thai flavours
text: Thai cooking balances four tastes: salty from fish sauce, sour from lime or tamarind, sweet from palm sugar, and often spicy from chilli, with bitter as a fifth element. A dish is adjusted until these are in harmony for its style. This deliberate balancing is central to Thai cuisine.

title: Guacamole
text: Guacamole is a Mexican dip of mashed ripe avocado seasoned with lime juice, salt, onion, chilli, and coriander. The lime juice adds flavour and slows browning of the avocado. It is best made fresh and kept covered, as the flesh oxidises and darkens on exposure to air.

title: Corn tortillas
text: Corn tortillas are made from masa, a dough of corn treated with an alkali in a process called nixtamalization, which develops flavour and makes nutrients available. The masa is pressed thin and cooked on a hot griddle until it puffs and sets. They are central to Mexican cooking.

title: Mole sauce
text: Mole is a family of complex Mexican sauces built from many ingredients, which may include several kinds of dried chilli, spices, nuts, seeds, dried fruit, and often a little chocolate. The ingredients are toasted, ground, and simmered into a deep, layered sauce. Mole poblano is among the best known.

title: Salsa fresca
text: Salsa fresca, or pico de gallo, is an uncooked Mexican relish of chopped tomato, onion, chilli, coriander, and lime juice. Because it is raw and fresh, its bright, crisp character depends on ripe tomatoes and being made shortly before serving. It accompanies tacos, grilled meats, and many dishes.

title: Refried beans
text: Refried beans are cooked beans, usually pinto, mashed and fried in fat until thick and creamy. Despite the name they are fried only once; the term comes from a mistranslation of well-fried. Cooking them in flavoured fat with onion and seasoning deepens their taste. They are a staple side in Mexican cooking.

title: American barbecue
text: American barbecue cooks tough cuts of meat such as brisket, pork shoulder, and ribs slowly at low temperature over wood smoke for many hours. The long, gentle cooking breaks down connective tissue and infuses the meat with smoke, while a bark forms on the surface. It differs from quick, high-heat grilling.

title: Buttermilk fried chicken
text: Fried chicken is often soaked in buttermilk before coating, which seasons and tenderises the meat and helps the flour crust adhere. The floured chicken is fried in hot oil until the coating is deep golden and crisp and the meat reaches a safe internal temperature. Maintaining oil temperature keeps the crust crisp, not greasy.

title: Beef chili
text: Chili con carne is a spiced stew of beef, chilli, and often beans and tomato, simmered slowly so the flavours meld and the meat becomes tender. Dried chillies and spices such as cumin build its warmth. Long, gentle cooking develops the deep, savoury flavour characteristic of a good chili.

title: Food danger zone
text: The temperature danger zone is roughly 5 to 60C (40 to 140F), the range in which bacteria multiply fastest. Perishable foods should not sit in this zone for more than about two hours. Keeping cold food below 5C and hot food above 60C, and cooling leftovers quickly, limits bacterial growth.

title: Preventing cross-contamination
text: Cross-contamination is the transfer of harmful bacteria from raw foods, especially raw meat, poultry, and seafood, to ready-to-eat foods. It is prevented by using separate cutting boards and utensils, washing hands and surfaces after handling raw items, and storing raw meat below other foods so it cannot drip onto them.

title: Safe defrosting
text: Frozen food should be thawed safely in the refrigerator, in cold running water, or in the microwave if cooked immediately, never at room temperature, where the outer surface warms into the bacterial danger zone while the centre is still frozen. Refrigerator thawing is slowest but safest.

title: Storing leftovers
text: Cooked food should be cooled quickly and refrigerated within about two hours, ideally divided into shallow containers so it cools fast. Most leftovers keep three to four days refrigerated and should be reheated thoroughly to steaming hot before serving. Freezing extends storage but does not improve safety of already-spoiled food.

title: Common substitutions
text: Many ingredients have reliable substitutes: buttermilk can be mimicked by adding lemon juice or vinegar to milk, self-raising flour by adding baking powder to plain flour, and a beaten egg can help bind mixtures. Substitutions work best when the replacement matches the original's role, whether acidity, leavening, fat, or moisture.

title: Measuring by weight
text: Weighing ingredients on a scale is more accurate than measuring by volume, especially for baking, where the density of an ingredient like flour varies with how it is scooped. Professional and European recipes usually give weights, while volume measures such as cups are common in the United States.

title: Volume conversions
text: Common volume conversions include three teaspoons to a tablespoon and sixteen tablespoons to a US cup. A US cup is about 240 millilitres, while an imperial pint is 568 millilitres and a US pint 473 millilitres. Because cup measures vary by country, weighing is more reliable for precise results.

title: Oven temperature conversions
text: Oven temperatures convert between systems: a moderate oven is about 180C, 350F, or gas mark 4. To convert Celsius to Fahrenheit, multiply by nine, divide by five, and add thirty-two. Fan or convection ovens run hotter, so recipes usually advise lowering the set temperature by about twenty degrees Celsius.

title: Chef knife use
text: A chef's knife is the most versatile kitchen knife, used for chopping, slicing, and dicing. A sharp blade is safer than a dull one because it cuts predictably with less force. Guiding the food with curled fingertips in a claw grip protects the fingers, and a rocking motion speeds chopping.

title: Cast iron cookware
text: Cast iron pans retain and distribute heat well and, once seasoned with baked-on oil, develop a naturally non-stick surface. They suit searing, frying, and baking. They should be dried thoroughly and lightly oiled after washing to prevent rust, and harsh scrubbing that strips the seasoning is avoided.

title: Non-stick pans
text: Non-stick pans release food easily and suit delicate cooking such as eggs and fish. Their coating is damaged by metal utensils and very high heat, so they are used with wooden or silicone tools over moderate heat. They are less suited to high-heat searing, where an uncoated pan browns food better.

title: Fixing a broken emulsion
text: A broken emulsion, such as a split mayonnaise or hollandaise, can often be rescued by starting again with a fresh base, an egg yolk or a spoonful of water, and slowly whisking the broken mixture into it drop by drop. Working gradually lets the droplets re-disperse and the sauce come back together.

title: Rescuing over-salted food
text: Over-salted dishes cannot have salt removed, but the saltiness can be diluted by adding more unsalted liquid or bulk, such as extra stock, water, or vegetables, or balanced with acidity or a little sweetness. Adding a raw potato does little; increasing the volume of the dish is the reliable fix.

title: Why food sticks
text: Food often sticks because the pan or the food is too cold or too wet, or because it is moved before a crust has formed. Proteins bond to the metal until browning is complete, then release naturally. Preheating the pan, drying the food, using enough fat, and waiting for release all prevent sticking.

title: Bloom of gelatin
text: Gelatin sheets or powder are softened, or bloomed, in cold water before use so they hydrate evenly, then dissolved into a warm liquid, never a boiling one, which can weaken their setting power. Gelatin sets desserts such as panna cotta and jelly, giving a tender, melting texture when used in the right amount.

title: Kneading bread dough
text: Kneading works bread dough to align and strengthen the gluten strands so the dough becomes smooth, elastic, and able to trap gas. It is done by stretching and folding the dough repeatedly until it passes the windowpane test, stretching thin without tearing. Wetter doughs need gentler folding rather than vigorous kneading.

title: Windowpane test
text: The windowpane test checks whether bread dough has been kneaded enough by stretching a small piece thin. If it forms a translucent membrane without tearing, the gluten is well developed; if it tears easily, the dough needs more kneading. It confirms the dough can stretch to trap fermentation gases.

title: Soffritto
text: Soffritto is the Italian aromatic base of finely chopped onion, carrot, and celery cooked slowly in olive oil until soft and sweet, forming the flavour foundation of many sauces, soups, and braises such as ragu. Gentle, unhurried cooking develops depth without browning the vegetables harshly.

title: Deglazing versus reducing
text: Deglazing lifts flavour from a pan with liquid, while reducing then simmers that liquid to concentrate it. The two steps often follow one another: deglaze to capture the fond, then reduce to build body and intensity before finishing the sauce. Together they turn pan residue into a concentrated sauce.

title: Veal cuts
text: Veal is meat from young cattle, paler and more tender than beef with a mild, delicate flavour. Tender cuts such as loin and rib suit quick cooking, while the shank makes osso buco and tougher shoulder is braised. Because veal is lean and lacks the fat of mature beef, it dries out easily and is often cooked with moisture or sauce.

title: Osso buco
text: Osso buco is a Milanese braise of cross-cut veal shanks cooked slowly in wine, stock, and vegetables until the meat is tender and the marrow in the central bone softens. It is traditionally finished with gremolata, a mix of lemon zest, garlic, and parsley, which brightens the rich dish. It is often served with saffron risotto.

title: Gremolata
text: Gremolata is an Italian garnish of finely chopped parsley, garlic, and lemon zest, sprinkled over rich dishes such as osso buco to cut through their richness. It is added raw at the end so its fresh, sharp aroma is preserved. The lemon zest provides brightness without the wetness of juice.

title: Carving against the grain
text: Meat is more tender when sliced across, or against, the grain, meaning perpendicular to the direction of the muscle fibres. This shortens the fibres in each bite so less chewing is needed. It matters most for coarse-grained cuts such as brisket, flank, and skirt, where slicing with the grain leaves long, stringy fibres.

title: Trussing a bird
text: Trussing ties the legs and wings close to a bird's body with string, giving a compact, even shape for roasting. This helps it cook more uniformly and look neat, though a loosely trussed or untrussed bird lets more hot air reach the thighs, which can help them finish alongside the breast.

title: Basting roasts
text: Basting spoons pan juices or fat over roasting meat to add flavour and colour to the surface. It does little to keep the interior moist, since the liquid runs off, and repeatedly opening the oven lowers the temperature and lengthens cooking. It is most useful for building a glossy, well-coloured skin.

title: Reverse searing
text: Reverse searing cooks a thick steak or roast gently in a low oven until it nears the target temperature, then finishes it with a hard sear for a crust. This gives even doneness edge to edge and a dry surface that browns quickly, avoiding the overcooked grey band a hot pan alone can produce.

title: Marinades
text: A marinade seasons and flavours the surface of food and can be built from oil, acid, salt, and aromatics. Acids and enzymes tenderise only the outermost layer, so marinating chiefly adds flavour rather than penetrating deeply. Prolonged acidic marinades can turn the surface of fish or meat mushy.

title: Dry rubs
text: A dry rub is a mixture of salt, spices, and sometimes sugar massaged onto meat before cooking to season it and build a flavourful crust. Applied ahead, the salt draws out and reabsorbs moisture, seasoning deeper. Sugar in a rub aids browning but can burn over very high or prolonged heat.

title: Larding and barding
text: Larding threads strips of fat through lean meat, while barding wraps it in a layer of fat such as bacon or caul, both to keep lean cuts moist during roasting. As the fat melts it bastes the meat internally or externally. These older techniques suit very lean cuts prone to drying out.

title: Cooking bacon
text: Bacon can be fried, grilled, or baked. Starting it in a cold pan lets the fat render slowly for even crisping, while baking on a tray gives flat, evenly cooked rashers with less spatter. The rendered fat is flavourful and can be saved. Cooking too fast over high heat burns the edges before the fat renders.

title: Sausage cooking
text: Sausages are cooked gently so the interior reaches a safe temperature before the outside burns, since high heat splits the casing and dries them. Poaching or baking then browning, or cooking slowly in a pan, gives even results. Pricking is usually unnecessary and lets out juices and fat.

title: Meatballs
text: Meatballs are made from ground meat bound with egg and often breadcrumbs soaked in milk, called a panade, which keeps them tender and moist. Overworking the mixture makes them dense, so it is handled lightly. They can be browned then simmered in sauce, which finishes cooking them and flavours the sauce.

title: Burgers
text: A good burger uses ground beef with around twenty percent fat, formed into patties with a light touch to keep them tender. A dimple pressed into the centre stops the patty doming as it cooks. Seasoning the outside just before cooking and searing over high heat builds a browned, flavourful crust.

title: Shepherd's and cottage pie
text: Shepherd's pie is made with minced lamb and cottage pie with minced beef, each topped with mashed potato and baked until the top is browned. The meat is cooked with onion, stock, and often vegetables into a savoury base. The distinction is the meat: shepherds tend flocks, hence lamb for shepherd's pie.

title: Steak and kidney
text: Steak and kidney is a British filling of diced beef and kidney stewed slowly in a rich gravy until tender, used in pies and puddings. The long braise softens the tough beef and mellows the kidney. In a steamed pudding it is encased in suet pastry; in a pie, in shortcrust or puff.

title: Pot roast
text: A pot roast braises a large, tough cut such as beef chuck or brisket slowly in a covered pot with a little liquid and vegetables. The moist, gentle heat over hours breaks down the connective tissue into gelatin, making the meat tender and creating a rich sauce from the reduced cooking liquid.

title: Corned beef
text: Corned beef is beef, usually brisket, cured in a seasoned brine with salt and often pickling spices, which preserves it and gives a distinctive flavour and pink colour. It is then simmered slowly until tender. The name comes from the corns, or coarse grains, of salt once used to cure it.

title: Pancetta and guanciale
text: Pancetta is Italian cured pork belly and guanciale is cured pork cheek or jowl, both salted and aged but not smoked. Guanciale is fattier with a deeper flavour and is the authentic choice for carbonara and amatriciana, while pancetta is a common substitute. Rendering either releases flavourful fat.

title: Prosciutto
text: Prosciutto is Italian dry-cured ham, salted and air-dried for many months or years until it can be sliced paper-thin. Prosciutto crudo is eaten raw as an antipasto, its flavour concentrated by the long curing. It is often paired with melon or figs and added at the end of cooked dishes to preserve its delicacy.

title: Chorizo
text: Chorizo is a pork sausage seasoned with paprika, which gives its red colour and smoky flavour. Spanish chorizo is cured and firm, eaten sliced or cooked, while fresh Mexican chorizo is soft and cooked from raw. Cooking releases its coloured, flavourful fat, which can be used to cook other ingredients.

title: Roasting vegetables with meat
text: Vegetables roasted alongside a joint absorb the rendered fat and juices, gaining flavour, though they should be sized so they finish with the meat. Potatoes for roasting are often parboiled and roughened first so their edges crisp. Crowding the pan steams rather than browns, so a single layer with space is best.

title: Yorkshire pudding
text: Yorkshire pudding is a batter of flour, egg, and milk baked in very hot fat until it puffs dramatically and crisps. The key is a smoking-hot pan of fat and a rested batter, so the sudden heat sets the outside as steam inflates the centre. It traditionally accompanies roast beef.

title: Gravy from a roast
text: Roast gravy uses the fat and browned juices left in the pan. Excess fat is poured off, flour is cooked in the remaining fat and drippings to a roux, then stock and deglazed pan residue are whisked in and simmered until smooth and thickened. Straining and seasoning give a glossy sauce for the roast.

title: Spatchcock roast timing
text: A spatchcocked chicken roasts faster than a whole bird because it lies flat and the heat reaches more of the surface. At a high temperature a spatchcocked chicken can roast in around forty-five minutes, with crisp skin and the breast and thighs finishing closer together than in an upright bird.

title: Chicken kiev
text: Chicken kiev is a chicken breast wrapped around a core of garlic and herb butter, breaded, and fried or baked. When cut, the melted butter flows out. Sealing the butter fully inside the breaded coating is essential, or it leaks during cooking. Chilling the parcel before cooking helps it hold together.

title: Chicken schnitzel
text: Schnitzel is a thin, pounded cutlet, coated in flour, egg, and breadcrumbs and shallow-fried until golden and crisp. Pounding the meat thin ensures it cooks through before the crumb burns. The classic Wiener schnitzel uses veal, but chicken and pork are common. A squeeze of lemon finishes it.

title: Chicken stock versus broth
text: Stock is made chiefly from bones, giving a gelatin-rich, savoury liquid used as a cooking base, while broth is made more from meat and is often seasoned to be drunk on its own. In practice the terms overlap, but a good stock sets to a jelly when chilled thanks to the gelatin drawn from the bones.

title: Deep-frying temperature
text: Deep-frying works best at around 175 to 190C. Too cool and food absorbs oil and turns greasy; too hot and the outside burns before the inside cooks. A thermometer or the sizzle test keeps the oil steady, and frying in small batches prevents the temperature dropping too far when food is added.

title: Choosing frying oil
text: Frying needs an oil with a high smoke point, such as vegetable, sunflower, groundnut, or refined rapeseed oil, which stay stable at high heat. Oils with low smoke points, like extra virgin olive oil or butter, break down and smoke, giving off-flavours. Fresh oil and a steady temperature keep fried food crisp.

title: Poaching versus boiling
text: Poaching cooks food in liquid held just below a simmer, around 70 to 80C, with barely any movement, keeping delicate foods such as eggs and fish intact. Boiling at a rolling 100C is too violent for these and would break them up. The gentle heat of poaching suits anything easily damaged.

title: Court bouillon
text: Court bouillon is a quickly made aromatic poaching liquid of water with vegetables, herbs, and usually an acid such as wine or vinegar. It is used to poach fish and shellfish, lending gentle flavour. Unlike stock it is not simmered for long, since its purpose is a flavourful bath rather than a concentrated base.

title: Beurre noisette
text: Beurre noisette, or brown butter, is butter cooked until its milk solids toast to a golden-brown and it develops a nutty aroma. It adds rich, nutty depth to sauces, pasta, fish, and baking. It goes quickly from browned to burnt, so it is watched closely and removed from the heat as soon as it smells nutty.

title: Emulsion basics
text: An emulsion suspends tiny droplets of one liquid, such as oil, within another it would normally separate from, such as water or vinegar. An emulsifier like egg yolk or mustard coats the droplets and keeps them dispersed. Emulsions underpin mayonnaise, hollandaise, vinaigrette, and butter sauces.

title: Thickening with cornflour
text: Cornflour, or cornstarch, thickens sauces when mixed first with cold liquid into a slurry, then stirred into the hot dish, where it clears and thickens as it comes to a simmer. Unlike a flour roux it gives a glossy, translucent finish. Overcooking or too much acid can thin a cornflour-thickened sauce.

title: Thickening with a beurre manie
text: Beurre manie is equal parts soft butter and flour kneaded into a paste, whisked into a simmering sauce at the end to thicken it. Because the flour is coated in fat, it disperses without lumping. It is a quick fix for a thin sauce, unlike a roux which is made at the start of a dish.

title: Making stock clear
text: A clear stock comes from a gentle simmer, never a hard boil, which would churn fat and particles into the liquid and cloud it. Starting bones in cold water, skimming the scum that rises, and not stirring keep it clear. Straining slowly through fine cloth at the end removes the last impurities.

title: Skimming stocks and soups
text: As stocks and soups heat, proteins and impurities rise to the surface as foam or scum, which is skimmed off to keep the liquid clean and clear. Fat also rises and can be skimmed or lifted off once chilled, when it sets solid. Regular skimming during a long simmer improves flavour and clarity.

title: Bloom on chocolate
text: Bloom is the dull, streaky or whitish film that appears on chocolate. Fat bloom comes from cocoa butter recrystallising after warming, and sugar bloom from moisture dissolving and redepositing sugar. Bloomed chocolate is safe to eat but looks and snaps poorly; proper tempering and cool, dry storage prevent it.

title: Whipping cream
text: Cream whips when its fat, which must be at least about thirty percent, traps air as it is beaten, stiffening into a foam. Cold cream, bowl, and beaters whip faster and hold better. Over-whipping pushes the fat to clump, first turning the cream grainy and then, if continued, into butter and buttermilk.

title: Folding batter
text: Folding gently combines a light, aerated mixture such as whipped whites or cream with a heavier one while preserving the trapped air. A spatula cuts down through the centre, sweeps along the bottom, and lifts over, turning the bowl between strokes. Vigorous stirring instead would deflate the air and yield a dense result.

title: Creaming butter and sugar
text: Creaming beats softened butter with sugar until pale and fluffy, forcing air into the fat which the sugar crystals help trap. This aeration gives cakes and cookies their rise and light texture. Butter that is too cold will not aerate, and melted butter cannot hold air, so it should be soft but not oily.

title: Resting cake batter
text: Some batters benefit from resting, which lets the flour hydrate and the gluten relax and, for chemically leavened batters, allows bubbles to develop, though many are baked promptly so the leavening is not spent. Pancake batter often rests to relax gluten for tender results, while whisked sponges are baked at once.

title: Docking pastry
text: Docking pricks small holes in rolled-out pastry with a fork so steam can escape during baking, preventing the base from puffing up unevenly. It is used when a flat, crisp base is wanted. For a pie case that must stay flat under a filling, docking is combined with weighting the case during blind baking.

title: Egg wash
text: An egg wash is beaten egg brushed onto pastry or bread before baking to give a glossy, golden-brown finish. The proteins and sugars in the egg brown in the heat. Whole egg gives a deep shine, yolk a darker gloss, and white a lighter, crisper glaze. It can also seal edges and hold on toppings.

title: Proving in the fridge
text: A cold, slow prove in the refrigerator, sometimes overnight, slows the yeast so flavour develops more fully while the dough rises gradually. This retarding suits pizza, sourdough, and enriched doughs, deepening taste and making the timing more flexible. The cold dough is often easier to shape as well.

title: Oven spring
text: Oven spring is the rapid final rise a loaf makes in the first minutes of baking, as the trapped gases expand and the yeast has a last burst of activity before the heat kills it and the crust sets. Good oven spring depends on proper proving, a hot oven, and, for lean breads, steam.

title: Pizza margherita
text: Pizza margherita is a Neapolitan pizza topped simply with tomato, mozzarella, and basil, its colours said to echo the Italian flag. Baked very quickly in a scorching oven, the base blisters and the cheese just melts. Good ingredients and a hot oven matter more than complexity in this classic.

title: Neapolitan pizza
text: True Neapolitan pizza is baked in a wood-fired oven at around 450 to 480C for only sixty to ninety seconds, giving a soft, puffy, charred rim and a thin, tender centre. The dough is a simple flour, water, salt, and yeast mixture, slowly fermented and stretched by hand. Its style is closely defined by tradition.

title: Calzone
text: A calzone is a folded pizza, a round of dough filled with ingredients such as ricotta, mozzarella, and cured meats, sealed into a half-moon and baked. Because it is enclosed, the filling steams, so wetter ingredients are used sparingly to avoid a soggy interior. A vent lets steam escape during baking.

title: Fresh egg pasta
text: Fresh egg pasta is made from flour and eggs kneaded into a smooth dough, rested to relax the gluten, then rolled thin and cut. The eggs give richness and a tender bite. It cooks in just a few minutes, far faster than dried pasta, and suits filled shapes and ribbons such as tagliatelle and ravioli.

title: Ravioli and filled pasta
text: Ravioli and other filled pastas enclose a filling between thin sheets of fresh pasta, sealed with care to expel air pockets that could burst in cooking. Fillings such as ricotta and spinach or meat are kept fairly dry so they do not soften the pasta. They are cooked gently so the seals hold.

title: Orecchiette with broccoli
text: Orecchiette with broccoli rabe is a dish from Puglia in which the little ear-shaped pasta is tossed with the slightly bitter greens, garlic, chilli, and anchovy or olive oil. The greens are often cooked in the same water as the pasta. The dish balances the bitterness of the rabe with savoury garlic and chilli.

title: Spaghetti alle vongole
text: Spaghetti alle vongole is a Neapolitan dish of pasta with clams, garlic, olive oil, white wine, and parsley, sometimes with a little tomato. The clams are opened in the pan and their briny liquor becomes the sauce, emulsified with oil and pasta water. It is served the moment the clams open, before they toughen.

title: Ragu versus bolognese
text: Ragu is the broad Italian term for a slow-cooked meat sauce, of which bolognese from Bologna is one regional example. Southern ragus, such as Neapolitan, may braise large cuts of meat slowly in tomato, while bolognese uses minced meat with little tomato and some milk. All rely on long, gentle cooking.

title: Reserving pasta water
text: The starchy water pasta cooks in is reserved before draining and used to loosen and emulsify sauces. Its dissolved starch helps oil and fat bind into a glossy sauce that clings to the pasta, as in cacio e pepe or aglio e olio. A little added at a time brings a sauce to the right consistency.

title: French onion caramelisation
text: The deep flavour of French onion soup comes from cooking sliced onions slowly, often for an hour, so their sugars caramelise to a rich brown. Rushing over high heat scorches rather than caramelises them. A little salt draws out moisture and a splash of liquid helps deglaze the browning as it builds.

title: Vichyssoise
text: Vichyssoise is a chilled soup of leeks and potato blended smooth and enriched with cream, served cold. It is essentially a refined, cold version of leek and potato soup. The potato gives body when pureed, and the soup is well seasoned since chilling dulls the perception of salt.

title: Bisque
text: A bisque is a rich, smooth soup traditionally made from shellfish such as lobster or crab, whose shells are simmered to extract flavour and then the soup is thickened and enriched with cream. Historically rice thickened it. The shells are the key to its deep seafood flavour, and the soup is strained silky.

title: Borscht
text: Borscht is an Eastern European soup coloured deep red by beetroot, served hot or cold and often with a spoon of sour cream. It may include cabbage, potato, and meat in heartier versions. A little acidity, from vinegar or the beets themselves, brightens the earthy sweetness of the beetroot.

title: Pho
text: Pho is a Vietnamese noodle soup built on a clear, aromatic broth simmered for hours with beef or chicken bones, charred onion and ginger, and spices such as star anise and cinnamon. It is served over rice noodles with thin slices of meat, and finished at the table with herbs, lime, chilli, and bean sprouts.

title: Tom yum
text: Tom yum is a hot and sour Thai soup flavoured with lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaves, lime juice, fish sauce, and chilli, often with prawns. The aromatics are simmered to infuse the broth, then balanced sour, salty, and spicy. It is bright and fragrant rather than long-simmered and heavy.

title: Cullen skink
