text: Cullen skink is a Scottish soup of smoked haddock, potato, onion, and milk or cream, thick and hearty. The smoked fish gives it a distinctive savoury depth. The potato thickens the soup, and the fish is added gently so it stays in flakes rather than breaking down completely.

title: Reducing a stock to glace
text: A stock reduced very far, until it becomes syrupy and coats a spoon, forms a glace, or meat glaze, an intensely flavoured concentrate. A small amount enriches sauces with deep, savoury body. Because reduction concentrates everything, the base stock should be unsalted so the glaze does not turn overly salty.

title: Allspice
text: Allspice is the dried berry of a Caribbean tree, so named because its warm aroma suggests a blend of cinnamon, clove, and nutmeg. It is central to Caribbean jerk seasoning and Middle Eastern cooking and features in baking and pickling. A little goes a long way, as its flavour is potent.

title: Cardamom
text: Cardamom is an intensely aromatic spice from the pods of a ginger relative, with a warm, floral, slightly citrusy flavour. Green cardamom is used in both sweet and savoury Indian and Scandinavian cooking, while black cardamom is smoky and savoury. The whole pods or seeds are often bruised or ground to release the aroma.

title: Cloves
text: Cloves are the dried flower buds of a tropical tree, with a strong, warm, sweet, and slightly numbing flavour. Used whole or ground, they flavour spiced meats, mulled drinks, baking, and studded hams. Their potency means they are used sparingly, as too many turn a dish bitter and medicinal.

title: Fennel seed
text: Fennel seed has a sweet, aniseed-like flavour and is used in Italian sausage, pork dishes, breads, and Indian spice blends. Toasting brings out its sweetness. It pairs naturally with pork and oily fish, cutting through richness, and the seeds are sometimes chewed as a digestive after meals.

title: Fenugreek
text: Fenugreek is used both as small hard seeds and as leaves, called methi. The seeds have a slightly bitter, maple-like aroma and are a defining note of many curry powders, while the leaves add a savoury depth to Indian dishes. The seeds are toasted carefully, as over-toasting makes them harshly bitter.

title: Mustard seed
text: Mustard seeds are pungent when crushed and moistened, as this releases the compounds responsible for their heat. Whole seeds are tempered in hot oil in Indian cooking, where they pop and turn nutty, while ground mustard flavours sauces and pickles. Heat mellows their sharpness, so mustard is often added late.

title: Sichuan peppercorn
text: Sichuan peppercorn is not a true pepper but the husk of a prickly ash berry, producing a tingling, numbing sensation on the tongue rather than heat. It is essential to the mala flavour of Sichuan cooking. The husks are often toasted and ground, and the shiny black seeds inside are discarded as gritty.

title: Vanilla
text: Vanilla is the cured seed pod of an orchid, prized for its warm, floral, sweet aroma. The tiny seeds and the pod both carry flavour, and the pod can be split and steeped in warm liquid. Real vanilla is costly, so extract and, less desirably, synthetic vanillin are common substitutes in baking.

title: Za'atar
text: Za'atar is a Middle Eastern blend of dried wild thyme or oregano, sumac, toasted sesame seeds, and salt, tangy and herbaceous. It is sprinkled on flatbread with olive oil, over dips, and on roasted vegetables and meats. The sumac gives it a lemony sourness that distinguishes it from a plain herb mix.

title: Sumac
text: Sumac is a deep red spice ground from dried berries, with a tart, lemony flavour and no heat. It is used across Middle Eastern cooking to add brightness to grilled meats, salads such as fattoush, dips, and rice, and is a component of za'atar. It provides sourness without the moisture of citrus juice.

title: Harissa
text: Harissa is a North African chilli paste of roasted red chillies, garlic, and spices such as cumin, coriander, and caraway, blended with olive oil. It brings heat and depth to stews, couscous, marinades, and eggs. Its intensity varies, so it is added gradually to reach the desired warmth.

title: Ras el hanout
text: Ras el hanout is a complex North African spice blend that can contain a dozen or more spices, its name meaning head of the shop, implying the seller's finest mix. It typically includes warm spices such as cinnamon, cumin, coriander, ginger, and cardamom, and flavours tagines, couscous, and grilled meats.

title: Berbere
text: Berbere is an Ethiopian spice blend built around dried chilli with warm and aromatic spices such as fenugreek, ginger, cardamom, and allspice. It is fiery and deeply flavoured and forms the base of stews called wat. The spices are often toasted before grinding to deepen their aroma.

title: Blooming spices in oil
text: Ground spices release more of their flavour when bloomed in hot fat, which dissolves their fat-soluble aromatic compounds and spreads them through a dish. Spices are added to the pan for a short time until fragrant, before liquids go in, taking care not to let them scorch and turn bitter.

title: Curry paste versus powder
text: Curry pastes, common in Thai cooking, are wet blends of fresh aromatics such as lemongrass, galangal, and chilli pounded together, while curry powders are dry ground spice mixes. Pastes are usually fried in oil to release their aroma before liquid is added, whereas powders can be bloomed similarly or added to a dish.

title: Storing spices
text: Ground spices lose their aroma within months as their volatile oils fade, while whole spices keep far longer and are best ground as needed. Spices are stored in airtight containers away from heat, light, and moisture, such as not directly above the stove, where warmth accelerates the loss of flavour.

title: When to add herbs
text: Hardy, woody herbs such as rosemary, thyme, and bay are added early so their flavour infuses the dish during cooking, while tender herbs such as basil, parsley, coriander, and chives are added at the end or as a garnish, since heat quickly dulls their fresh, volatile aromas.

title: Chinese velveting
text: Velveting is a Chinese technique of coating sliced meat in a mixture of egg white, cornflour, and sometimes rice wine, then briefly blanching it in oil or water before stir-frying. The coating protects the meat from the fierce heat, keeping it tender and silky. It is why restaurant stir-fried meat is so smooth.

title: Char siu
text: Char siu is Cantonese barbecued pork, strips of pork marinated in a sweet and savoury mixture of hoisin, honey, soy, and five-spice, then roasted until caramelised and glazed at the edges. The sugar in the marinade produces its characteristic reddish, lacquered exterior. It is served sliced with rice or in buns.

title: Peking duck
text: Peking duck is a Beijing speciality prized for its crisp, lacquered skin. The duck is air-dried, often after its skin is separated from the flesh and coated with a sugar solution, then roasted until the skin crackles. It is served with thin pancakes, spring onion, cucumber, and sweet bean sauce.

title: Wok hei
text: Wok hei, meaning the breath of the wok, is the smoky, seared aroma imparted to stir-fried food by a searing-hot wok. It arises when food and oils briefly contact the intensely hot metal and flames. Achieving it needs high heat, a hot wok, small batches, and dry ingredients, so the food sears rather than steams.

title: Congee
text: Congee is a savoury rice porridge cooked by simmering rice in a large amount of water or stock until the grains break down into a smooth, thick porridge. Eaten across Asia, it is often topped with savoury garnishes such as spring onion, ginger, meat, or preserved egg. Long, gentle cooking gives its creamy texture.

title: Onigiri
text: Onigiri are Japanese rice balls of seasoned or plain cooked rice pressed into a triangle or ball, often with a savoury filling and wrapped in a strip of nori. The rice must be the sticky short-grain type so it holds together. They are a common portable snack and lunch item.

title: Gyoza
text: Gyoza are Japanese dumplings, usually filled with pork and cabbage, most often cooked by the potsticker method: fried on one side until crisp, then steamed with a splash of water in a covered pan until cooked through. This gives a crisp base and a tender, steamed top. They are served with a dipping sauce.

title: Katsu
text: Katsu is a Japanese cutlet of pork or chicken coated in panko breadcrumbs and deep-fried until golden and crisp. Panko gives an especially light, crunchy crust. It is served sliced, often with a thick, sweet and savoury tonkatsu sauce, and appears in dishes such as katsu curry and the katsudon rice bowl.

title: Panko breadcrumbs
text: Panko are Japanese breadcrumbs made from crustless bread, coarse and flaky rather than fine. They absorb less oil and stay crisper and lighter than ordinary breadcrumbs, giving a delicate, crunchy coating on fried foods such as katsu and prawns. Their airy structure is what makes them prized for frying.

title: Bibimbap
text: Bibimbap is a Korean rice bowl topped with an array of seasoned vegetables, often meat, and a fried or raw egg, with gochujang chilli paste stirred in before eating. Served in a hot stone bowl, the rice against the sides forms a crisp crust. The dish is mixed thoroughly at the table, as its name suggests.

title: Kimchi
text: Kimchi is Korean fermented vegetables, most famously napa cabbage salted and coated in a paste of chilli, garlic, ginger, and often fish sauce, then left to ferment. The lactic acid fermentation gives it a sour, tangy, spicy flavour and preserves it. It is a staple side dish and an ingredient in many cooked dishes.

title: Gochujang
text: Gochujang is a thick, fermented Korean chilli paste made from chilli powder, glutinous rice, fermented soybeans, and salt. It is spicy, savoury, and slightly sweet, with deep umami from the fermentation. It flavours stews, marinades, and sauces, and is stirred into dishes such as bibimbap. A little adds both heat and depth.

title: Tacos al pastor
text: Tacos al pastor are made from pork marinated in chillies and spices, stacked on a vertical spit with pineapple and cooked as it turns, then shaved off. The method descends from Lebanese shawarma. The thin slices are served in small corn tortillas with onion, coriander, and a little of the pineapple.

title: Enchiladas
text: Enchiladas are corn tortillas dipped in a chilli sauce, wrapped around a filling such as meat, cheese, or beans, then baked in more sauce with cheese on top. The tortillas are usually softened in warm sauce or oil first so they roll without cracking. The sauce keeps them moist as they bake.

title: Tamales
text: Tamales are a Mesoamerican dish of masa dough spread with a filling, wrapped in a corn husk or banana leaf, and steamed until firm. The steaming cooks the masa into a tender, cohesive dough around the filling. The wrapper is peeled away before eating and is not consumed.

title: Ceviche
text: Ceviche is a Latin American dish of raw fish or seafood cured in citrus juice, usually lime, whose acidity denatures the proteins so the flesh turns opaque and firm as if cooked. It is mixed with onion, chilli, and coriander and served fresh. Because the fish is not heated, it must be very fresh and handled cleanly.

title: Jambalaya
text: Jambalaya is a Louisiana rice dish of the Creole and Cajun traditions, cooking rice together with meat such as sausage and chicken, seafood, and the aromatic trinity of onion, celery, and pepper in a seasoned, often tomato-tinged base. The rice absorbs the flavourful liquid as it cooks in one pot.

title: Gumbo
text: Gumbo is a Louisiana stew thickened by a dark roux, and sometimes okra or file powder, combining ingredients such as sausage, chicken, or seafood with the trinity of onion, celery, and pepper. The roux is cooked slowly to a deep brown for its characteristic nutty flavour and colour, served over rice.

title: Cajun trinity
text: The holy trinity of Cajun and Creole cooking is diced onion, celery, and green bell pepper, cooked as the aromatic base of dishes such as gumbo, jambalaya, and etouffee. It is the Louisiana counterpart to the French mirepoix, with green pepper standing in for carrot, and underpins the region's cuisine.

title: Cornbread
text: Cornbread is a quick bread leavened with baking powder or soda, made from cornmeal with some flour, giving a crumbly, slightly sweet or savoury loaf. Southern versions tend to be less sweet and are often baked in a hot cast iron skillet greased with fat for a crisp crust. It pairs with chilli and barbecue.

title: Clam chowder styles
text: New England clam chowder is creamy and thickened with milk or cream and potatoes, while Manhattan clam chowder is tomato-based and brothy without dairy. Both feature clams and their liquor. Rhode Island offers a clear, brothy version. The style is defined chiefly by whether it uses cream, tomato, or neither.

title: Grits and polenta
text: Grits and polenta are both porridges of ground maize simmered in liquid until thick and creamy. Grits, common in the American South, are usually made from a starchier dent corn, while Italian polenta is typically coarser flint corn. Both need long, stirred cooking and can be served soft or set and grilled.

title: Deglazing for cream sauces
text: For a pan cream sauce, meat is browned, the fond deglazed with stock or wine, then cream is added and simmered until it thickens by reduction. The cream must not boil hard or it can split, and acidic deglazing liquid is reduced enough before the cream goes in to reduce the risk of curdling.

title: Preventing curdled cream
text: Cream and milk can curdle when heated with acid or boiled hard. Reducing acidic liquids before adding dairy, using higher-fat cream which is more stable, warming dairy gently, and stabilising with a little starch all help. Once split, a sauce can sometimes be smoothed by blending, but prevention is easier.

title: Refreshing herbs
text: Limp fresh herbs and leafy greens can often be revived by soaking in cold water, which rehydrates their cells so they become crisp again. Tender herbs such as parsley and coriander keep well stored upright in a jar of water like flowers, loosely covered, in the refrigerator.

title: Blanching and shocking
text: Blanching briefly boils vegetables, then shocking plunges them into iced water to stop the cooking and set their bright colour. It is used to par-cook vegetables, loosen skins for peeling, and prepare greens for freezing. The rapid cooling preserves crispness and vivid colour and halts the softening from residual heat.

title: Deep green vegetables and acid
text: Green vegetables lose their bright colour and turn drab olive when cooked too long or in acidic water, as acid degrades their chlorophyll. Cooking them quickly in plenty of boiling water, uncovered, and not adding acid until serving helps them stay vividly green. Overcooking is the most common cause of dullness.

title: Peeling tomatoes
text: Tomatoes are peeled easily by scoring a small cross in the skin, blanching in boiling water for a few seconds until the skin loosens, then plunging into iced water. The skin then slips off readily. This is useful when a smooth sauce or a skinless texture is wanted, as tomato skins do not soften in cooking.

title: Roasting garlic
text: Roasting garlic whole, wrapped or in its skin, transforms its harsh raw pungency into a mellow, sweet, spreadable paste as the sugars caramelise slowly in gentle heat. The soft cloves squeeze out easily. Roasted garlic enriches dips, dressings, mash, and sauces with depth but without the bite of raw garlic.

title: Toasting nuts
text: Toasting nuts in a dry pan or oven until fragrant and lightly golden deepens their flavour and makes them crisp. They burn quickly once they start to colour, so they are watched closely and stirred. The residual heat continues cooking them, so they are removed a touch before they look fully done.

title: Making breadcrumbs
text: Fresh breadcrumbs are made by blitzing slightly stale bread, giving soft crumbs for binding or toppings, while dried breadcrumbs are made from fully dried bread for a crisp coating. Stale bread crumbs more cleanly than fresh, which can turn gummy. Toasting breadcrumbs in fat gives a golden, crunchy garnish.

title: Deveining prawns
text: Deveining removes the dark digestive tract running along a prawn's back by making a shallow cut and lifting it out. It is done for appearance and because the vein can be gritty, though it is harmless if eaten. Shells can be left on for cooking to add flavour and protect the flesh, then removed before eating.

title: Shucking oysters
text: Oysters are opened, or shucked, by working a short, sturdy knife into the hinge at the pointed end and twisting to pop the shell, then sliding the blade along the top shell to cut the muscle. It is done carefully with a protected hand. The oyster is kept in its liquor, which carries much of its briny flavour.

title: Cleaning mussels
text: Mussels are scrubbed under cold water and debearded by pulling away the fibrous threads that anchor them. Any with cracked shells, or open ones that do not close when tapped, are discarded before cooking as they may be dead. Live, tightly closed mussels are the ones to cook.

title: Salt cod
text: Salt cod, or bacalao, is cod preserved by salting and drying, which draws out moisture and concentrates flavour. It must be soaked in several changes of cold water over a day or more to rehydrate and remove excess salt before cooking. It features in Portuguese, Spanish, and Italian dishes such as brandade.

title: Curing salmon into gravlax
text: Gravlax is salmon cured, not cooked, by burying a fillet in a mixture of salt, sugar, and dill for a day or two under weight. The salt and sugar draw out moisture and firm the flesh, giving a silky, lightly sweet cure. It is sliced thin and served with a mustard-dill sauce.

title: Frying fish batter
text: For crisp battered fish, a thin batter, often with cold sparkling water or beer for lightness, coats the fish which is then lowered into hot oil around 180C. The batter sets quickly into a crisp shell that steams the fish inside. Cold batter and hot oil give the lightest, crispest result.

title: Grilling lobster
text: Lobster is often parboiled or steamed briefly, then split and finished on the grill so the flesh does not overcook and toughen. Basting the exposed meat with butter keeps it moist. Lobster is done when the flesh is opaque and firm; overcooking makes it rubbery and dry.

title: Steaming crab
text: Crabs are cooked live by steaming or boiling until the shell turns bright and the meat is set, then cooled and picked. Steaming preserves more flavour than boiling, which can leach it into the water. The cooked meat is sweet and delicate and is used in cakes, salads, and dressed crab.

title: Anchovies in cooking
text: Anchovies, whether salt-packed or in oil, melt into a dish when gently cooked, dissolving into the fat and adding deep savoury umami without a fishy taste. They enrich sauces such as puttanesca, dressings such as Caesar, and braises, functioning as a background seasoning rather than an obvious flavour.

title: Umami
text: Umami is the savoury fifth basic taste, produced mainly by glutamates and certain nucleotides found in foods such as aged cheese, tomatoes, mushrooms, cured meats, soy sauce, and stock. Combining umami-rich ingredients deepens the savoury character of a dish. It is why these ingredients make food taste fuller and more satisfying.

title: Acid in cooking
text: Acidic ingredients such as lemon juice, vinegar, and wine brighten dishes, balance richness and sweetness, and lift flavours that taste flat. A squeeze of acid at the end often makes a dish taste more complete. Acids also tenderise surfaces, curdle dairy, and help set some emulsions.

title: Balancing sweet and sour
text: Many cuisines balance sweetness and sourness for a rounded flavour, as in sweet and sour sauces, agrodolce, and Thai dishes. A little sugar can soften harsh acidity, while acid can cut cloying sweetness. Adjusting the two against each other, along with salt, is a core way of tuning a dish to taste.

title: Bitterness in food
text: Bitterness, from ingredients such as dark greens, coffee, citrus pith, and some spices, adds complexity and can balance richness and sweetness. It is often tempered with fat, salt, or a touch of sweetness rather than removed entirely. A measured amount of bitterness keeps a rich dish from tasting flat.

title: Fat as flavour carrier
text: Fat carries and distributes many flavour compounds that dissolve in it but not in water, which is why blooming spices in oil, or the fat in a sauce, spreads their taste through a dish. Fat also gives richness and mouthfeel, so some fat in a dish helps its flavours register fully on the palate.

title: Resting batter for gluten
text: Resting a flour batter, as for pancakes, crepes, or Yorkshire pudding, lets the flour fully hydrate and the gluten relax, giving a smoother batter and a more tender result. Without resting, the gluten can make the cooked product tough or rubbery. A rest of thirty minutes to an hour is common.

title: Water bath baking
text: A bain-marie, or water bath, surrounds a delicate baked custard such as creme brulee or cheesecake with hot water in the oven, moderating and evening out the heat so the eggs set gently without curdling or cracking. The water keeps the temperature at or below the boiling point around the dish.

title: Preventing meringue weeping
text: Meringue can weep beads of syrup or shrink if underbaked, if sugar is not fully dissolved, or from humidity. Dissolving the sugar completely, adding it gradually, cooking the meringue enough, and avoiding damp conditions help. A little cornflour or acid can stabilise softer meringues on pies.

title: Making pastry cream set
text: Pastry cream is thickened with starch, which must be brought to a full boil for a minute or so to cook out the raw taste and let it set properly, unlike a plain custard which is kept below boiling. The starch also protects the yolks from curdling, allowing the higher temperature.

title: Tempering method for chocolate
text: One common tempering method is seeding: melting chocolate, then stirring in finely chopped tempered chocolate as it cools, which introduces stable cocoa butter crystals to guide the rest to set correctly. The chocolate is worked to a precise temperature that differs for dark, milk, and white chocolate.

title: Ganache
text: Ganache is a smooth mixture of chocolate and warm cream, used as a filling, glaze, or, when set and whipped, a frosting. The ratio of chocolate to cream sets its firmness: more chocolate gives a firmer ganache for truffles, more cream a pourable glaze. The cream is warmed and poured over the chocolate to melt it.

title: Genoise sponge
text: A genoise is a whisked sponge in which whole eggs and sugar are warmed and beaten to a thick foam, then flour and often melted butter are folded in. It relies wholly on the beaten-in air for lift, with no chemical leavener. Gentle folding preserves the foam, and it is often soaked in syrup as it can be dry.

title: Swiss and Italian meringue
text: Swiss meringue is made by warming egg whites and sugar together over a bain-marie until the sugar dissolves, then whisking to stiff peaks, giving a dense, stable foam. Italian meringue is made by whisking hot sugar syrup into whipping whites, which cooks and stabilises them, useful for buttercream and toppings.

title: Roux for gumbo
text: The dark roux that defines Cajun gumbo is cooked slowly, sometimes for an hour, stirring constantly, until it reaches a deep brown the colour of chocolate, developing a nutty, toasted flavour. The darker it cooks the less it thickens, so a dark roux is used more for flavour and colour than as a thickener.

title: Trussing versus spatchcocking
text: Trussing ties a bird into a compact shape for even browning and presentation, while spatchcocking removes the backbone and flattens it for faster, more even cooking and crisper skin. They serve opposite goals: trussing tightens the bird, spatchcocking opens it out. The choice depends on the cooking method and desired result.

title: Duck fat roast potatoes
text: Roast potatoes cooked in duck fat crisp especially well because the fat has a high smoke point and rich flavour. The potatoes are parboiled, roughed up to create craggy surfaces, then roasted in hot fat until deeply golden and crisp outside and fluffy within. Duck or goose fat is prized for the flavour it lends.

title: Confit garlic
text: Confit garlic is whole peeled cloves cooked slowly submerged in oil at a low temperature until soft, sweet, and spreadable. The gentle cooking mellows the garlic and infuses the oil with flavour. Both the soft cloves and the garlic oil are used in cooking. It is kept refrigerated and used within a short time for safety.

title: Deglazing with wine
text: Wine is a common deglazing liquid, its acidity and flavour dissolving the fond and adding brightness and depth to a sauce. It is usually cooked for a minute or two to drive off the raw alcohol and soften its sharpness before other liquids or cream are added. Both red and white wines suit different dishes.

title: Sofrito in Spanish cooking
text: Sofrito in Spanish and Latin cooking is a slowly cooked base of aromatics, typically onion, garlic, and tomato, sometimes with pepper, fried gently in oil until soft and concentrated. It forms the flavourful foundation of rice dishes, stews, and sauces. Long, patient cooking deepens its sweetness and richness.

title: Tomato paste
text: Tomato paste is tomatoes cooked down to a thick, concentrated puree, adding deep, sweet tomato flavour and umami with little liquid. Frying it briefly in oil, a step called caramelising or cooking out, darkens it and removes any raw, tinny taste, deepening its flavour before it is stirred into a dish.

title: Passata and canned tomatoes
text: Passata is smooth, sieved uncooked tomatoes, ideal for a quick smooth sauce, while canned whole or chopped tomatoes give more texture and are often preferred by cooks for their reliable ripeness. Good canned tomatoes, picked and packed ripe, frequently make a better sauce out of season than fresh ones.

title: Reducing tomato sauce
text: A tomato sauce is simmered to reduce excess water, concentrating flavour and thickening it to coat pasta. Cooking gently and uncovered, or partly covered to limit spattering, lets moisture escape while the flavours meld. A long, slow simmer sweetens the sauce, while a quick reduction keeps it fresh and bright.

title: Bechamel for lasagne
text: In lasagne, bechamel adds creaminess and moisture, binding the layers and preventing dryness. It is made a little looser than a coating sauce so it stays creamy after baking. Seasoned with nutmeg and combined with Parmesan, it complements the ragu, and its milk gives the dish a silky richness.

title: Mornay sauce
text: Mornay is a derivative of bechamel enriched with grated cheese, typically Gruyere and Parmesan, melted into the warm white sauce. It is used for gratins, cauliflower cheese, and croque monsieur. The cheese is stirred in off strong heat so it melts smoothly without becoming stringy or oily.

title: Sauce supreme
text: Sauce supreme is a derivative of veloute made with chicken stock and enriched with cream, giving a rich, smooth white sauce for poultry. It shows how the mother sauces branch into families: a base veloute becomes supreme with cream, or allemande when finished with egg yolk. The stock's quality shapes the result.

title: Bearnaise sauce
text: Bearnaise is a derivative of hollandaise, made the same way with an emulsion of egg yolk and butter but flavoured with a reduction of vinegar, shallots, and tarragon instead of lemon. It classically accompanies grilled steak. Like hollandaise, gentle heat is essential to keep the emulsion from breaking.

title: Aioli
text: Aioli is a garlic emulsion sauce from the Mediterranean, in its traditional form garlic pounded with salt and emulsified with olive oil, and in common usage a garlic mayonnaise. It is served with fish, vegetables, and bread. The strong garlic flavour is central, and, like mayonnaise, the oil is added slowly to emulsify.

title: Romesco
text: Romesco is a Catalan sauce of roasted red peppers, tomatoes, garlic, almonds or hazelnuts, and often bread, blended with olive oil and vinegar into a thick, nutty, smoky sauce. It accompanies grilled vegetables, especially calcots, and fish and meat. The toasted nuts give it body and richness.

title: Pesto variations
text: Beyond the classic basil pesto alla genovese, many variations exist: pesto rosso with sun-dried tomatoes, pesto alla trapanese from Sicily with almonds and tomato, and versions using other herbs or greens such as rocket or parsley. All share the method of grinding herbs or greens with oil, nuts, cheese, and garlic.

title: Salsa verde Italian
text: The Italian salsa verde is a piquant green sauce of parsley, capers, anchovy, garlic, and olive oil, often with a little vinegar or mustard, served with boiled meats, fish, and vegetables. It is chopped or pounded rather than smoothly blended, keeping some texture. Its sharp, salty brightness cuts through rich foods.

title: Pico de gallo versus salsa
text: Pico de gallo is a chunky, fresh, uncooked salsa of diced tomato, onion, chilli, and coriander with little liquid, while many other salsas are blended and sometimes cooked, giving a smoother, saucier texture. Pico is used as a fresh relish, whereas cooked or blended salsas pour more readily over dishes.

title: Marinara sauce
text: Marinara is a simple, quick tomato sauce of tomatoes cooked with garlic, olive oil, and herbs, without meat. In its Neapolitan origin it is a fast sauce, and the name is thought to relate to sailors. Its brief cooking keeps a bright, fresh tomato flavour, distinguishing it from long-simmered ragus.

title: Puttanesca ingredients
text: The character of puttanesca comes from its briny, pungent ingredients: anchovies, capers, and olives with garlic and chilli in a tomato base. These provide plenty of salt and savour, so little or no extra salt is needed. The sauce comes together quickly and is boldly flavoured rather than subtle.

title: Amatriciana versus gricia
text: Amatriciana is essentially the older Roman pasta gricia, made of guanciale and Pecorino, with tomato added. Gricia itself has no tomato. Both render the guanciale for its fat and toss the pasta with Pecorino. Understanding the family, gricia, amatriciana, carbonara, and cacio e pepe, shows how a few ingredients recombine.

title: Carbonara without cream
text: Authentic carbonara contains no cream; its silky sauce comes from egg yolks and grated Pecorino emulsified with the heat of the pasta and a little starchy cooking water. Adding the eggs off the heat, while tossing, cooks them into a creamy coating without scrambling. Cream is a common but inauthentic shortcut.

title: Pasta shapes and sauces
text: Pasta shapes are matched to sauces by how well they hold them: long strands such as spaghetti suit oil- or cream-based sauces that coat them, while tubes and ridged shapes such as rigatoni or penne trap chunky and meaty sauces. Small shapes suit soups. The pairing helps every bite carry sauce.

title: Cooking dried versus fresh pasta
text: Dried pasta, made from durum wheat and water, cooks in around eight to twelve minutes and gives a firm bite, while fresh egg pasta cooks in just two to four minutes and is more tender. They are not always interchangeable, as fresh pasta suits delicate sauces and filled shapes, dried pasta robust ones.

title: Finishing pasta in sauce
text: Draining pasta a little before it is fully cooked and finishing it in the sauce for the last minute lets it absorb flavour and helps the sauce cling, bound by the pasta's released starch and a splash of cooking water. This mantecatura-like step gives a more cohesive dish than simply spooning sauce over plain pasta.

title: Fresh pasta hydration
text: The ratio of egg to flour and the flour type determine fresh pasta's texture. A common guide is one egg to about a hundred grams of flour. Too little liquid gives a dry, crumbly dough; too much a sticky one. The dough is kneaded until smooth and rested so the gluten relaxes for easy rolling.

title: Semolina for pasta
text: Semolina, the coarse flour milled from hard durum wheat, gives pasta a firm bite and pale gold colour and is standard for dried pasta. It is also dusted on fresh pasta and pizza peels to stop sticking. Its high protein content forms strong gluten that holds shape through cooking without turning soft.

title: Making stock from scraps
text: Vegetable trimmings such as onion skins, carrot peel, celery ends, and herb stalks, and leftover roast bones, can be saved and simmered into a flavourful stock, reducing waste. Strongly flavoured or bitter scraps such as brassica trimmings are used sparingly. The scraps can be frozen until enough accumulate for a batch.

title: Freezing stock
text: Homemade stock freezes well and can be stored in portions, or reduced and frozen as concentrated cubes to save space, then diluted when used. Cooling it quickly before freezing and labelling it helps. Frozen stock keeps for months and gives home cooking a depth that water or cubes cannot match.

title: Bone broth
text: Bone broth is a stock simmered especially long, often many hours, to extract as much gelatin and minerals from the bones as possible, giving a rich, body-filled liquid that sets firmly when chilled. Adding a little acid such as vinegar is thought to help draw minerals from the bones during the long cook.

title: Roasting bones for stock
text: Roasting bones and vegetables before simmering them gives a brown stock with deeper colour and richer, more complex flavour through the Maillard browning, compared with a pale white stock from raw bones. The roasting caramelises the surfaces, and a little tomato paste can add further depth to a brown stock.

title: Clarifying butter for sauces
text: Clarified butter is preferred in some sauces and for high-heat cooking because removing the milk solids raises its smoke point and gives a cleaner, purer butter flavour that will not brown or burn as readily. It is made by melting butter and separating the clear fat from the foam and the milky sediment.

title: Emulsifying with mustard
text: Mustard is a natural emulsifier used in vinaigrettes and sauces because its compounds help oil and acid stay mixed, stabilising the emulsion so the dressing does not separate as quickly. It also adds flavour and a little heat. A small spoonful whisked into a vinaigrette makes a creamier, more stable dressing.

title: Vinaigrette ratio
text: A classic vinaigrette uses roughly three parts oil to one part acid, adjusted to taste and to the sharpness of the vinegar. Salt is dissolved in the acid first, then oil is whisked in to emulsify, often with mustard to help. The balance can be tuned toward more or less acid depending on the dish.

title: Infused oils
text: Oils can be infused with flavour from herbs, garlic, chilli, or spices, either gently warmed or steeped, to make a seasoned oil for finishing or cooking. Because low-acid ingredients such as garlic in oil can pose a botulism risk if stored, infused oils, especially with fresh aromatics, are best made fresh and kept cold.

title: Compound butter
text: Compound butter is softened butter blended with flavourings such as herbs, garlic, citrus zest, or spices, then chilled. A slice melted over grilled meat, fish, or vegetables adds instant richness and flavour. It can be rolled in paper into a log, chilled, and sliced as needed, and freezes well.

title: Deglazing for gravy
text: After roasting meat, the browned residue in the pan is the foundation of gravy. Excess fat is poured off, then liquid is added and the fond scraped up and dissolved, capturing that concentrated flavour before the gravy is thickened and simmered. Skipping this step wastes much of the roast's flavour.

title: Making jus
text: A jus is a light, unthickened sauce made from the natural juices of roasted meat, often extended with a little stock and reduced for flavour rather than thickened with flour. It is more delicate than gravy, letting the pure meat flavour show. Straining and skimming give a clean, glossy sauce.

title: Cornstarch versus flour thickening
text: Cornstarch thickens with about twice the power of flour and gives a glossy, clear result, set into a slurry and added late, while flour gives a more opaque, matte sauce and is usually cooked as a roux from the start. Cornstarch-thickened sauces can thin if boiled too long or held hot, while flour-based ones are more stable.

title: Sabayon and zabaglione
text: Zabaglione, or sabayon, is a light, frothy custard made by whisking egg yolks, sugar, and a wine such as Marsala over gentle heat until thick, pale, and voluminous. The constant whisking incorporates air while the gentle heat cooks the yolks without scrambling. It is served warm as a dessert or sauce.

title: Creme anglaise
text: Creme anglaise is a pourable vanilla custard sauce of milk or cream, egg yolks, and sugar, cooked gently while stirred until it thickens just enough to coat the back of a spoon, around 80C. It must not boil or the eggs curdle. It is served over desserts and is the base for many ice creams.

title: Ice cream custard base
text: A rich ice cream begins with a cooked custard of cream, milk, sugar, and egg yolks, chilled then churned while freezing to incorporate air and keep ice crystals small. The yolks add richness and help keep the texture smooth. Churning is what gives ice cream its soft, scoopable body rather than a solid block.

title: Sorbet
text: Sorbet is a frozen dessert of fruit puree or juice with sugar and water, containing no dairy. The sugar concentration is important: too little and it freezes rock hard, too much and it will not set. Churning keeps the crystals fine and the texture smooth, giving a light, intensely fruity result.

title: Panna cotta setting
text: Panna cotta relies on just enough gelatin to set the cream so it barely holds its shape and wobbles when turned out, melting on the tongue. The gelatin is bloomed then dissolved in warm, not boiling, cream. Too much gelatin makes it rubbery; too little and it will not unmould cleanly.

title: Souffle
text: A souffle rises because whisked egg whites folded into a flavoured base expand as the trapped air and steam heat in the oven. It must be baked promptly and undisturbed, as knocks or an opened oven can deflate it, and it begins to sink soon after leaving the oven, so it is served immediately.

title: Custard tart
text: A baked custard tart is a pastry case filled with a set custard of eggs, cream or milk, and sugar, often dusted with nutmeg. The pastry is usually blind-baked first so the base stays crisp, and the custard is baked gently until just set with a slight wobble, since overbaking curdles it and makes it grainy.

title: Tarte tatin
text: Tarte tatin is an upside-down French tart of caramelised apples baked under a pastry lid, then inverted so the glossy caramelised fruit is on top. The fruit is cooked in butter and sugar to a caramel in the pan before the pastry is laid over and the whole baked, then flipped out while warm.

title: Lemon curd
text: Lemon curd is a smooth, tangy spread cooked from lemon juice and zest, sugar, eggs, and butter, stirred gently over low heat until thickened by the eggs. It must not boil or the eggs scramble. Straining gives a silky texture. It fills tarts and cakes and is spread on scones and toast.

title: Choux for profiteroles
text: Profiteroles are small choux buns baked until crisp and hollow, then filled with cream or custard and often coated in chocolate. The choux must be baked long enough to dry out inside, or it collapses as it cools. Piping even mounds and not opening the oven early help them rise evenly and stay puffed.

title: Puff pastry lamination
text: Puff pastry's rise comes from lamination: dough and butter folded through repeated turns to build many thin layers. Keeping everything cold stops the butter melting into the dough, which would ruin the layers. In the oven, steam from the butter's water pushes the layers apart, creating the flaky, risen structure.

title: Rough puff pastry
text: Rough puff is a quicker alternative to full puff pastry, made by mixing chunks of cold butter roughly into the flour, then rolling and folding a few times to create some layers. It rises less dramatically than classic puff but is far faster, and it suits pie lids and tarts where perfect layers are not essential.

title: Shortcrust for tarts
text: Sweet shortcrust, or pate sucree, adds sugar and often egg yolk to shortcrust for a firmer, biscuit-like tart shell. Keeping the fat cold and the handling minimal keeps it tender, and chilling the shaped case before baking limits shrinkage. It is usually blind-baked before a wet filling is added.

title: Preventing soggy pastry bottoms
text: A soggy pastry base is avoided by blind baking the case first, brushing the baked base with egg white or a thin layer of melted chocolate to seal it, and baking on a preheated tray or pizza stone so heat hits the bottom directly. Not overfilling with wet filling before the base has set also helps.

title: Scones
text: Scones are a quick bread leavened with baking powder, made by rubbing cold butter into flour, then binding with milk into a soft dough handled as little as possible. Overworking develops gluten and makes them tough. The dough is cut, not twisted, so the scones rise straight and evenly in a hot oven.

title: Pancake batter
text: Pancake batter of flour, egg, and milk is mixed just until combined, as overmixing develops gluten and toughens the result. Resting the batter relaxes the gluten and hydrates the flour for tender pancakes. Thin batters make crepes, while thicker batters with a raising agent make fluffy American-style pancakes.

title: Crepes
text: Crepes are very thin pancakes made from a loose batter poured into a hot pan and swirled to coat it thinly, cooked briefly on each side. A rested batter and a well-heated, lightly greased pan give lacy, tender crepes. They can be filled sweet or savoury, as with the classic crepe suzette in an orange sauce.

title: Waffles
text: Waffles are made from a batter similar to pancakes, often with more fat and sometimes whisked egg whites for lightness, cooked in a hot waffle iron that gives their crisp, gridded surface. The pockets hold syrup and butter. A hot iron and enough fat in the batter produce a crisp exterior and tender interior.

title: Doughnuts
text: Yeast doughnuts are a light, enriched dough proved then deep-fried, puffing and browning quickly in hot oil, while cake doughnuts are chemically leavened and denser. The oil must be at the right temperature so the doughnut cooks through without absorbing too much fat or burning outside before the centre sets.

title: Cheesecake baking
text: Baked cheesecake is a custard of soft cheese, eggs, and sugar set gently in the oven, often in a water bath, so it cooks evenly without cracking. It is baked until just set with a slight wobble in the centre, then cooled slowly, as sudden temperature changes and overbaking cause cracks. Chilling firms it fully.

title: Brownies
text: Brownies range from fudgy to cakey depending on the ratio of fat and chocolate to flour and eggs and how much they are beaten. Fudgy brownies have more fat and less flour and are baked just until set, while more flour and beaten eggs give a cakier crumb. Underbaking slightly keeps them moist and dense.

title: Cookies spreading
text: How much a cookie spreads depends on butter temperature, sugar type, and flour. Melted or very soft butter and more white sugar spread more, giving thin, crisp cookies, while cold dough, more flour, or brown sugar spread less for thicker, chewier ones. Chilling the dough reduces spread and deepens flavour.

title: Caramel stages
text: Sugar cooked for caramel passes through stages of increasing colour and flavour, from pale gold to deep amber, growing more bitter and complex as it darkens. It is watched closely near the end, as it goes from perfect to burnt in seconds. A candy thermometer or careful observation of colour guides the cook.

title: Wet versus dry caramel
text: A wet caramel is made by dissolving sugar in water first, then boiling until it colours, which is more forgiving and less prone to crystallising, while a dry caramel melts sugar alone, which is faster but can burn or crystallise more easily. Both reach the same amber caramel but by different, temperature-sensitive routes.

title: Preventing sugar crystallisation
text: Crystallisation, where a smooth syrup turns grainy, is discouraged by keeping stray sugar crystals off the pan sides, adding a little acid such as lemon juice or an interfering sugar such as glucose, and not stirring once the sugar has dissolved. A lid early on lets steam wash down the sides.

title: Tempering chocolate temperatures
text: Dark chocolate is typically melted to around 45C, cooled to about 27C to form crystals, then rewarmed to roughly 31C to work with, while milk and white chocolate use slightly lower temperatures. Hitting these ranges encourages the stable cocoa butter crystal form that gives a glossy, snappy set.

title: Melting chocolate gently
text: Chocolate scorches and seizes easily, so it is melted gently over a bain-marie or in short bursts in a microwave, stirring often. A small amount of water can cause smooth melted chocolate to seize into a stiff paste, so bowls and utensils are kept dry, though a larger amount of liquid can be safely incorporated.

title: Bread flour versus plain flour
text: Bread flour has a higher protein content, forming more gluten for a strong, chewy structure that holds gas, making it ideal for yeast breads. Plain, or all-purpose, flour has less protein, giving tenderer results suited to cakes, pastry, and general cooking. Using the right flour affects a recipe's texture markedly.

title: Cake flour
text: Cake flour is a low-protein, finely milled flour that produces a tender, fine crumb in delicate cakes because it forms little gluten. When unavailable, it can be approximated by replacing some plain flour with cornflour. Its softness suits sponges and light cakes, where too much gluten would toughen the result.

title: Wholemeal flour
text: Wholemeal flour contains the whole wheat grain, including the bran and germ, giving a nuttier flavour, more fibre, and a denser texture. The bran cuts through gluten strands, so wholemeal breads rise less than white and often need more water and a longer rest. It is frequently blended with white flour for a lighter loaf.

title: Hydration in bread
text: Hydration is the ratio of water to flour in a dough, expressed as a percentage. Higher-hydration doughs are wetter and stickier and tend to give a more open, holey crumb, as in ciabatta, while lower-hydration doughs are firmer and easier to shape. The hydration level strongly influences a bread's texture.

title: Pre-ferments
text: A pre-ferment, such as a poolish, biga, or sponge, is a portion of dough fermented ahead and mixed into the final dough, deepening flavour and improving texture and keeping quality through the extra fermentation. It is a way to build the benefits of long fermentation into a bread without an overly long final rise.

title: Brioche
text: Brioche is a rich French bread made with a high proportion of butter and eggs, giving a soft, tender, almost cake-like crumb and golden colour. The butter is worked into a developed dough gradually, and the dough is often chilled to firm the butter for shaping. It is used for both sweet and savoury dishes.

title: Bagels
text: Bagels are a dense, chewy bread whose distinctive texture comes from boiling the shaped rings briefly before baking, which sets the crust and gelatinises the surface starch for a shiny, chewy exterior. A little malt or sugar in the boiling water adds colour and flavour. They are then baked until deep golden.

title: Pretzels
text: Pretzels get their dark, glossy crust and distinctive flavour from a dip in an alkaline solution, traditionally lye and at home baking soda, before baking. The alkali promotes browning and the characteristic taste. They are shaped into knots, sprinkled with coarse salt, and baked until deep mahogany brown.

title: Flatbread cooking heat
text: Many flatbreads such as pita, naan, and tortillas cook fast at very high heat, which sets the surface and, for leavened or moist doughs, flashes the internal moisture to steam so they puff. A blazing griddle, tandoor, or oven is key; too cool a surface gives a dry, tough, unpuffed bread.

title: Focaccia dimpling
text: Focaccia is dimpled by pressing the fingertips deep into the risen dough, creating wells that hold olive oil and toppings and give its characteristic craggy surface. The dimpling also releases some gas and helps the bread bake evenly. Generous oil in the wells and on the base gives a crisp, rich crust.

title: Pizza dough fermentation
text: Pizza dough develops flavour and extensibility through fermentation, often a slow, cold rise over one to three days, which lets the gluten relax so the dough stretches thin without tearing and builds a more complex taste. A well-fermented dough is easier to shape and bakes into a lighter, more digestible crust.

title: Stretching pizza dough
text: Pizza dough is stretched by hand rather than rolled, so the airy edge is preserved and gas is not pressed out. The dough is coaxed outward from the centre, leaving a raised rim, and gravity and gentle stretching over the knuckles thin the base. Rolling would flatten the crust and give a denser, cracker-like edge.

title: Braising basics
text: Braising cooks food, usually a tough cut, partly submerged in liquid in a covered pot at low heat for a long time. The meat is often browned first for flavour, then simmered gently until tender as its collagen melts. The liquid becomes a rich sauce, and the closed pot keeps the environment moist throughout.

title: Stewing versus braising
text: Stewing and braising both use gentle, moist heat over long periods, but stewing uses smaller pieces fully submerged in liquid, while braising uses larger cuts only partly covered. Both suit tough, collagen-rich cuts and yield tender meat in a flavourful sauce. The distinction is chiefly the size of the pieces and the amount of liquid.

title: Deglazing before braising
text: After browning meat and vegetables for a braise, the pan is deglazed so the flavourful browned fond is dissolved into the braising liquid rather than left behind or burnt. This captures the depth built during browning. Wine, stock, or water lifts the fond, forming the flavour base of the finished sauce.

title: Salt curing
text: Salt curing preserves food by drawing out moisture and creating an environment hostile to spoilage bacteria. It is the basis of bacon, ham, gravlax, and salt cod. The salt both preserves and seasons, and in dry curing the food is packed in salt, while in wet curing it is submerged in brine.

title: Pickling
text: Pickling preserves food in an acidic brine, either by immersing it in vinegar or by encouraging lactic fermentation that produces acid naturally, as in traditional sauerkraut and kimchi. The acidity inhibits spoilage organisms. Quick pickles are made by steeping vegetables in seasoned vinegar for a short time.

title: Fermentation in food
text: Fermentation uses microbes to transform food, producing acids, alcohol, or gases that preserve it and create new flavours. Lactic fermentation makes yoghurt, sauerkraut, and kimchi tangy, while yeast fermentation leavens bread and makes wine and beer. Controlled fermentation both preserves food and deepens its flavour and complexity.

title: Blanching before freezing
text: Vegetables are usually blanched briefly and cooled before freezing, which deactivates enzymes that would otherwise degrade their colour, flavour, and texture in the freezer. The short boil sets colour and slows quality loss, and rapid cooling stops the cooking. Blanched, well-drained vegetables freeze better than raw ones.

title: Freezer burn
text: Freezer burn is the dry, discoloured patches that form on frozen food when moisture evaporates from its surface into the freezer, caused by air exposure and temperature fluctuation. It is harmless but degrades flavour and texture. Wrapping food tightly and removing air, and keeping the freezer cold and steady, prevent it.

title: Resting dough versus proving
text: Resting a dough relaxes the gluten so it can be shaped or rolled without springing back, while proving is the rise during which yeast produces gas. A bread dough may be rested during shaping and proved for its rises. Confusing the two can lead to tough, hard-to-shape dough or under- or over-risen bread.

title: Knowing when meat is done
text: The most reliable way to judge meat doneness is an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part, away from bone, since colour and firmness are imprecise. Touch and juices give rough guides, but for safety with poultry, pork, and mince, and for precision with steaks and roasts, temperature is the surest test.

title: Thermometer calibration
text: A food thermometer can be checked for accuracy in ice water, which should read 0C, or in boiling water, which should read 100C at sea level, adjusting for altitude. Calibrating or noting the offset ensures readings are trustworthy, which matters for both food safety and precise doneness of meat and confections.

title: Altitude and boiling point
text: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude because of reduced air pressure, so foods cooked in boiling water take longer and baked goods and confections behave differently. Recipes and candy temperatures may need adjusting at elevation, and the lower boiling point is why high-altitude cooking often requires modification.

title: Salting meat ahead
text: Salting meat well before cooking, from forty minutes to a day ahead, allows the salt to be drawn in and season the interior, and helps the surface dry for better browning. Salting just before cooking, by contrast, leaves surface moisture that can hinder searing. Advance salting, or dry brining, improves flavour and texture.

title: Dry brining
text: Dry brining rubs salt directly onto meat or poultry and rests it, often uncovered in the refrigerator, so the salt seasons the meat throughout and dries the surface for crisp skin or a good sear. Unlike a wet brine it adds no water, concentrating rather than diluting flavour. It suits roasts, chicken, and steaks.

title: Wet brining
text: Wet brining soaks lean meat or poultry in a saltwater solution, seasoning it and helping it hold moisture during cooking by changing the muscle proteins so they retain more water. It suits pork chops and poultry prone to drying out. The meat is patted dry before cooking to allow the surface to brown.

title: Cooking with wine
text: Wine adds acidity, flavour, and depth to sauces, braises, and risottos. It is usually cooked to drive off the raw alcohol and mellow its sharpness, and the general guidance is to cook with wine pleasant enough to drink. Reducing wine concentrates its flavour, and both red and white suit different dishes.

title: Reducing wine in sauces
text: Wine added to a sauce is often reduced, simmered to evaporate much of its volume, which drives off harsh alcohol and concentrates its flavour and acidity into a more rounded, integrated taste. Reducing it before adding cream also lowers the risk of the acid curdling the dairy. The reduction adds body and depth.

title: Mounting sauce with butter
text: Mounting, or monter au beurre, whisks cold butter into a warm sauce off strong heat just before serving, so the butter emulsifies to give a glossy sheen, richer flavour, and slightly thicker body. The sauce must not be too hot or the butter melts and splits rather than emulsifying into a smooth finish.

title: Emulsified pan sauce
text: A quick pan sauce is emulsified by whisking cold butter into the reduced deglazed juices off high heat, binding the fat and liquid into a smooth, glossy sauce. A little of the meat's resting juices can be stirred back in. This simple technique turns pan drippings into a refined finishing sauce in minutes.

title: Skinning fish fillets
text: To skin a fish fillet, it is laid skin-side down and a knife slid between the flesh and skin at the tail, then pushed along while the skin is held taut, keeping the blade angled slightly toward the skin. A firm grip on the skin and a sharp knife make a clean separation with little waste.

title: Scaling fish
text: Fish are scaled by scraping against the direction the scales lie, from tail to head, with a scaler or the back of a knife, ideally in a sink or bag to contain the flying scales. Scaling is done before gutting and filleting when the skin is to be eaten. Rinsing afterward removes loose scales.

title: Butterflying meat
text: Butterflying cuts a thick piece of meat almost through and opens it out like a book, creating a thinner, even piece that cooks faster and more uniformly, or can be stuffed and rolled. It is used for chicken breasts, pork, and boned legs of lamb. The even thickness helps the meat cook through without drying the edges.

title: Frenching bones
text: Frenching trims the meat and fat from the ends of rib or chop bones to expose clean bone, giving a neat presentation on racks of lamb, pork, and rib chops. It is cosmetic rather than functional, and the trimmings can be saved for stock. The exposed bones are sometimes covered to prevent charring during roasting.

title: Tying a roast
text: A roast is tied with kitchen string into an even, compact shape so it cooks uniformly and holds together, especially when boned, rolled, or stuffed. Even loops at regular intervals keep the shape. Tying is removed before or after carving, and it helps a rolled joint keep its round cross-section during roasting.

title: Poaching poultry
text: Poaching poultry gently simmers it in flavoured liquid, keeping the meat exceptionally moist and tender, as for poached chicken breast. The liquid must stay below a boil so the meat does not toughen. The poaching liquid becomes a light stock. It suits dishes where succulent, unbrowned meat is wanted, such as salads.

title: Grilling versus broiling
text: Grilling cooks food over a heat source, as on a barbecue, while broiling, or grilling in British usage under a salamander, cooks it under one. Both use intense radiant heat to brown and cook quickly, suiting thin, tender cuts. The direction of heat differs, but both char and caramelise surfaces rapidly.

title: Resting fish
text: Fish is delicate and needs only a very brief rest, if any, after cooking, unlike large roasts, since it holds little residual heat and can quickly cool. A minute lets carryover finish gently cooked fish. Overcooking, not lack of resting, is the usual cause of dry fish, so it is best pulled slightly underdone.

title: Cooking octopus
text: Octopus is tough and needs either long, gentle simmering, often an hour or more, to become tender, or careful tenderising, after which it can be quickly grilled or charred for flavour. Simmering it slowly breaks down its connective tissue. Some cooks braise it in its own juices with aromatics until fork-tender.

title: Cleaning squid
text: Squid is cleaned by pulling the head and innards from the body tube, removing the transparent quill inside, and peeling off the thin skin. The tentacles are cut from the head above the eyes, and the hard beak in their centre is removed. The cleaned tube can be scored, cut into rings, or left whole.

title: Grilling whole fish
text: Whole fish grills well because the skin and bones protect the flesh and add flavour, and it holds together better than a fillet. The skin is oiled and the grate clean and hot so it does not stick, and the fish is left undisturbed until it releases. Scoring the sides helps it cook evenly and take on seasoning.

title: Baking fish in salt crust
text: A whole fish can be baked encased in a thick crust of salt, often bound with egg white, which insulates it and seasons it gently while sealing in moisture, steaming the fish in its own juices. The hardened crust is cracked off at the table, revealing perfectly moist, evenly seasoned flesh.

title: Handling raw shellfish safely
text: Live shellfish such as mussels, clams, and oysters must be kept cold and alive until cooking, discarding any that are dead, broken, or fail to close. Cooked shellfish that stay shut may not have been alive and are discarded. Raw oysters carry some risk and should come from safe, reputable sources.

title: Frying calamari
text: Calamari is floured or battered lightly and fried very quickly in hot oil, just a minute or two, so it stays tender, since squid toughens with more than brief high-heat cooking. The oil must be hot so the coating crisps fast. Overcrowding cools the oil and makes the calamari greasy and rubbery.

title: Roux colours
text: A roux darkens and changes character the longer it cooks: white roux is barely coloured for pale sauces, blond roux is light golden for veloutes, and brown roux is deeply coloured and nutty for gumbo and brown sauces. As it darkens it gains flavour but loses thickening power, so darker roux thicken less.

title: Seasoning a stew
text: A stew is seasoned gradually and tasted near the end, since long simmering concentrates flavours and salt, so adding all the salt early can leave it too salty after reduction. A final adjustment of salt, and often a splash of acid or fresh herbs, balances and brightens the finished dish before serving.

title: Skimming fat from stews
text: Fat rises to the surface of stews and braises and can be skimmed off during cooking with a spoon, or lifted off easily once the dish is chilled and the fat sets. Removing excess fat gives a cleaner-tasting, less greasy sauce. Some fat is left for flavour and richness, but a thick layer is usually taken off.

title: Building flavour bases
text: Many cuisines begin a dish with an aromatic base cooked in fat, such as the French mirepoix, Italian soffritto, Spanish sofrito, or Cajun trinity. Cooking these vegetables slowly draws out sweetness and lays a foundation of flavour on which soups, stews, sauces, and braises are built.

title: Toasting grains
text: Toasting grains such as rice for risotto or pilaf, or spices, in fat or a dry pan before adding liquid, develops a nutty aroma and can help the grains stay separate. For risotto, briefly toasting the rice, called tostatura, coats and lightly seals the grains before the stock is added ladle by ladle.

title: Deglazing risotto with wine
text: In risotto, wine is often added after toasting the rice and cooked until absorbed before the stock goes in, deglazing the pan and adding acidity and depth that balance the richness of the finished dish. The wine's sharpness cuts through the creamy starch, and cooking it off removes the raw alcohol.

title: Finishing risotto
text: Risotto is finished off the heat with cold butter and grated Parmesan beaten in vigorously, a step called mantecatura, which emulsifies the fat into the starch for a creamy, glossy texture. The risotto should be loose enough to spread slightly on the plate, described as all'onda, meaning wavy.

title: Salting at the table versus cooking
text: Salt added during cooking penetrates and seasons food from within, while salt added at the table sits on the surface and is tasted more sharply. Both have a place: cooking with salt builds integrated seasoning, while a finishing sprinkle of flaky salt adds bursts of flavour and texture on the surface.

title: Finishing salts
text: Finishing salts such as flaky sea salt or fleur de sel are added just before serving for their texture and bursts of salinity rather than to season throughout. Their crunchy crystals stand out on foods from steaks to caramels and salads. Because they dissolve slowly, they are wasted if stirred into cooking.

title: Soaking beans
text: Soaking dried beans overnight, or with a quick hot soak, hydrates them so they cook more evenly and a little faster and can improve digestibility. It is not strictly essential, as unsoaked beans cook with longer simmering. Discarding the soaking water and cooking in fresh water is common practice.

title: Cooking lentils
text: Lentils cook faster than most beans and usually need no soaking. Firmer types such as Puy or green lentils hold their shape for salads, while red and yellow lentils break down into a soft puree, ideal for dal and soups. They are simmered gently until tender, with salt and acid added toward the end.

title: Aquafaba
text: Aquafaba is the viscous liquid from cooked or canned chickpeas, which can be whipped like egg white into a foam and used as an egg substitute in meringues, mousses, and mayonnaise. Its dissolved proteins and starches let it trap air. It is a useful plant-based alternative where whipped egg white is called for.

title: Roasting chickpeas
text: Chickpeas can be roasted until crisp for a snack or salad topping by drying them well, tossing with oil and seasoning, and baking until golden and crunchy. Drying them thoroughly first is key to crispness, as surface moisture steams them soft. They crisp best in a hot oven and are seasoned after roasting.

title: Reheating rice safely
text: Cooked rice can harbour spores of a bacterium that survives cooking and produces toxins if the rice is left warm too long. Rice should be cooled quickly and refrigerated promptly, stored no more than a day or two, and reheated until piping hot. Leaving cooked rice at room temperature for long is the main risk.

title: Washing rice
text: Rinsing rice before cooking removes surface starch, giving separate, fluffy grains and a clearer cooking water, which is desirable for pilafs and plain steamed rice. For dishes where creaminess is wanted, such as risotto or paella, the rice is not rinsed so its starch thickens the dish. The choice depends on the result desired.

title: Absorption method for rice
text: The absorption method cooks rice in a measured amount of water that it soaks up completely, leaving fluffy, separate grains with no draining. The pot is covered and left undisturbed over low heat, then rested off the heat. Lifting the lid or stirring releases steam and can make the rice unevenly cooked or gummy.

title: Storing eggs
text: In many countries eggs are refrigerated, which slows spoilage, while in some they are kept at room temperature because they retain a protective coating not washed off during processing. A fresh egg sinks in water, while a very old one floats as its air cell grows. Eggs are best kept away from strong odours, which they absorb.

title: Egg freshness test
text: An egg's freshness can be roughly judged by placing it in water: a fresh egg lies flat on the bottom, an older one stands upright, and a stale one floats because the air cell inside enlarges as moisture is lost through the shell over time. Floating eggs are best discarded or checked carefully before use.

title: Separating eggs
text: Eggs separate most cleanly when cold, as the yolk is firmer and less likely to break, though whites whip to greater volume at room temperature. The yolk is passed between shell halves or cupped in the hand to let the white slip through. Even a trace of yolk in the whites prevents them whipping properly.

title: Room temperature eggs for baking
text: Eggs at room temperature incorporate more easily and trap more air when beaten, and blend more smoothly into batters, than cold eggs, which can firm up butter and cause curdling. Many baking recipes call for room-temperature eggs for a better rise and texture. Cold eggs can be warmed quickly in a bowl of warm water.

title: Coddled eggs
text: A coddled egg is cooked very gently in a covered dish, often set in hot water, until barely set, giving a soft, delicate texture. The low, indirect heat cooks it slowly without toughening. It is milder and softer than a boiled egg and is served warm, sometimes with butter and seasoning in the dish.

title: Egg in emulsions
text: Egg yolk is a powerful emulsifier because it contains lecithin, which coats oil droplets and keeps them suspended in liquid, making it central to mayonnaise and hollandaise. A single yolk can emulsify a large volume of oil if added slowly. This property is why yolk-based sauces are stable and creamy.

title: Overcooked egg smell
text: Overcooking eggs, as in hard-boiling too long, can produce a green-grey ring around the yolk and a sulphurous smell, caused by a reaction between iron and sulphur compounds at high heat. Cooking eggs only as long as needed and cooling them quickly in cold water prevents the discolouration and off odour.

title: Deglazing for gravy from a bird
text: After roasting poultry, the pan holds fat and browned juices that make excellent gravy. The fat is separated, a little used to cook flour into a roux, then stock and the deglazed juices are whisked in and simmered smooth. The concentrated roasting residue gives the gravy its savoury depth and colour.

title: Making a bouquet garni versus sachet
text: A bouquet garni bundles fresh herbs tied together for easy removal, while a sachet, or sachet d'epices, encloses herbs and spices, sometimes including peppercorns, in a cloth pouch. Both flavour a liquid and are lifted out before serving. A sachet suits smaller items like peppercorns that a simple herb bundle cannot hold.

title: Straining sauces
text: Straining a sauce through a fine sieve or chinois removes lumps, solids, and aromatics, giving a smooth, refined texture. Pressing the solids extracts flavour before discarding them. Straining is a hallmark of classical sauce-making, used for veloutes, purees, and reductions to achieve a silky, professional finish.

title: Passing soup through a sieve
text: For an especially smooth soup, a blended puree can be passed through a fine sieve to remove any fibres, skins, or lumps, leaving a velvety texture. The soup is pushed through with a ladle or spatula and the solids discarded. This extra step refines pureed vegetable soups and bisques to a luxurious smoothness.

title: Cream in soups
text: Cream added to a soup enriches it and softens sharp or acidic flavours, but it is stirred in near the end and not boiled hard, as high heat and acidity can cause it to split. Warming the cream and reducing acidity first helps. A swirl of cream at serving adds richness and a decorative finish.

title: Croutons
text: Croutons are cubes of bread crisped in fat or the oven, adding crunch and flavour to soups and salads. Tossing the bread in oil or butter and seasoning before baking or frying, and cooking until golden, gives even, crisp results. Stale bread crisps well and makes good use of bread that would otherwise be wasted.

title: Garnishing soups
text: A garnish adds contrast in flavour, texture, and colour to a soup, such as croutons, a swirl of cream or oil, fresh herbs, or toasted seeds. It lifts a smooth soup with crunch or brightness and makes the dish more appealing. The garnish is added just before serving so it stays fresh and crisp.

title: Cooling soup safely
text: Large pots of soup or stock cool slowly and can linger in the bacterial danger zone, so they are cooled quickly by dividing into shallow containers, setting the pot in an ice bath, or stirring, then refrigerated promptly. Cooling fast and refrigerating within a couple of hours limits bacterial growth in the leftovers.

title: Deglazing a roasting tin
text: A roasting tin holds concentrated browned juices after roasting meat. Setting it over a burner and adding liquid, then scraping and simmering, dissolves this fond into a flavourful base for gravy or jus. The tin's wide surface has caught much flavour, so deglazing it captures the essence of the roast.

title: Thickening soups with potato
text: Starchy vegetables such as potato thicken a soup naturally when blended, giving body without flour or cream. A potato simmered in the soup and pureed lends a smooth, velvety texture. This is why leek and potato soup is creamy without much added cream, relying on the potato's starch for its body.

title: Immersion blender safety
text: An immersion, or stick, blender purees soup directly in the pot, but the hot liquid can splash and scald, so the blade is kept fully submerged before switching on and the blender not lifted out while running. Working the blender around the pot ensures an even puree. It saves transferring hot liquid to a jug blender.

title: Blending hot liquids
text: Blending hot soup in a jug blender can force the lid off as steam expands, so the blender is filled only partway, the lid vented with a cloth held over the top, and the blend started slowly. This prevents dangerous splattering of scalding liquid. Letting the soup cool a little first further reduces the risk.

title: Deglazing to make demi-glace
text: In classical cooking, deeply reduced and deglazed juices contribute to demi-glace and rich sauces. Building these sauces relies on capturing every bit of browned flavour through deglazing, then reducing to concentrate it. The layering of browning, deglazing, and reduction is what gives classical brown sauces their profound depth.

title: Marbling in meat
text: Marbling is the fine flecks of fat within a muscle, distinct from the fat around it. It melts during cooking to baste the meat from within, adding juiciness, flavour, and tenderness. Well-marbled cuts such as ribeye stay succulent, which is why marbling is prized and used to grade beef quality.

title: Aging beef
text: Aging beef improves its tenderness and flavour. Dry aging holds the meat in controlled cold air for weeks, concentrating flavour and letting natural enzymes tenderise it while a dry crust forms and is trimmed away. Wet aging keeps it vacuum-sealed, tenderising without the flavour concentration or loss of dry aging.

title: Why lean meat dries out
text: Lean meat with little fat or connective tissue, such as chicken breast or pork loin, dries out easily because it has little internal fat to keep it moist and quickly passes the point of tenderness as its proteins tighten and expel water with heat. Such cuts are cooked briefly to a lower final temperature to stay juicy.

title: Grain of the meat
text: The grain is the direction in which a cut's muscle fibres run. Slicing across the grain shortens the fibres so each bite is more tender, while slicing along it leaves long, chewy strands. Identifying and cutting against the grain is especially important for coarse-grained cuts such as flank, skirt, and brisket.

title: Searing to build crust
text: Searing browns the surface of meat over high heat, driving the Maillard reaction to create a flavourful crust. It does not seal in juices, as once thought, but it builds deep flavour and appealing colour. A dry surface, a hot pan, and not moving the meat until it releases give the best crust.

title: Fond and its uses
text: Fond is the browned residue left in a pan after searing or roasting, rich in concentrated Maillard flavour. Far from being burnt waste, it is deglazed with liquid to form the flavour base of sauces and gravies. Building and then dissolving fond is a fundamental technique for adding depth to a dish.

title: Cooking to temperature not time
text: Cooking times are only guides, as they vary with the size, shape, and starting temperature of food and the true heat of the oven or pan. Judging doneness by internal temperature or clear physical signs is far more reliable, especially for meat and baking, where a few degrees change the result markedly.

title: Preheating pans and ovens
text: Preheating a pan or oven to the right temperature before adding food ensures proper searing, rising, and even cooking. Food added to a cold pan sticks and steams rather than browns, and baked goods put into a cool oven may spread or fail to rise. A properly heated cooking surface is fundamental to good results.

title: Overcrowding the pan
text: Crowding too much food into a pan lowers its temperature and traps released moisture, so the food steams and turns grey instead of browning. Cooking in batches, or using a larger pan, keeps the surface hot and dry so ingredients sear and caramelise. Space between pieces is essential for good browning.

title: Mise en place
text: Mise en place, meaning everything in its place, is the practice of preparing and organising all ingredients and equipment before cooking begins. It is essential for fast cooking such as stir-frying, where there is no time to chop mid-process, and it makes any cooking calmer, more accurate, and less error-prone.

title: Resting knife skills
text: Consistent knife cuts make food cook evenly, since uniform pieces reach doneness at the same time, while ragged pieces cook unevenly with some overdone and others raw. Basic cuts such as dice, julienne, and chiffonade give control over texture and cooking. A sharp knife and steady technique underpin good, safe preparation.

title: Sharpening versus honing
text: Honing with a steel realigns a knife's edge that has bent with use, keeping it cutting well, while sharpening actually removes metal to create a new edge on a stone or sharpener. Honing is done frequently and sharpening occasionally. A well-honed, periodically sharpened knife is safer and easier to use than a dull one.

title: Cutting boards and safety
text: Separate cutting boards for raw meat and for ready-to-eat foods such as vegetables prevent cross-contamination. Boards are washed thoroughly between different foods and after raw meat. A damp cloth under the board stops it slipping, and a claw grip on the food protects the fingers from the moving blade.

title: Choosing pots and pans
text: Different pans suit different tasks: heavy stainless or cast iron browns and holds heat for searing, non-stick suits eggs and delicate foods, and a wide pan aids evaporation for reductions while a tall pot suits boiling and stocks. Matching the pan's size and material to the job improves results and control.

title: Heavy-bottomed pans
text: A heavy-bottomed pan distributes heat evenly and holds it steadily, reducing hot spots that scorch food and helping maintain temperature when cold ingredients are added. It is preferred for searing, sauces, and anything prone to sticking or burning. Thin pans heat unevenly and cool quickly, making delicate cooking harder.

title: Wooden versus metal utensils
text: Wooden and silicone utensils are gentle on non-stick and enamelled surfaces, which metal can scratch, and wood does not conduct heat or react with acidic foods. Metal utensils suit uncoated pans and tasks needing a firm edge. Matching the utensil to the cookware protects the surface and the food.

title: Using a mandoline safely
text: A mandoline slices food thinly and uniformly, faster than a knife, but its sharp blade makes it a common cause of kitchen cuts. The guard or a protective glove holds the food safely away from the blade, especially as the piece grows small. Steady, careful strokes give even slices without risking the fingers.

title: Baking sheets and liners
text: Baking parchment and silicone mats line trays to stop food sticking and to ease cleaning, and give even browning.
